stories.body:
Gong simmers with rage, loneliness and humiliation as the ‘fourth mistress’ navigating the intimate political savagery of her husband’s compound in Zhang Yimou’s 1991 drama

R evisiting Zhang Yimou’s grippingly addictive psychological drama from 1991, adapted from a novella by Su Tong , is a reminder of what a great impact this movie made on western audiences. They responded to its arguably westernised tale of a young woman’s desperate loneliness in a sinister environment that resembles something by Charlotte Brontë or Daphne du Maurier. Like Jung Chang’s memoir Wild Swans from the same year, Raise the Red Lantern opened our eyes to 20th-century China’s secret theatre of cruelty and misogyny; elaborate domestic rituals of submission and servitude coexisted with infinitely subtle plotting, resentful manoeuvring and covert denunciation, habits of thought that could so easily be absorbed into Maoism.

Gong Li gives one of the great performances of the 1990s as Songlian, a beautiful, intelligent young woman in 1920s China who is forced to abandon her university studies after just six months because her father has died and there is no longer money for the fees. In the unforgettable opening scene, which unfolds with a single unbroken shot of Gong’s pale face, incandescent with shock and pain, Songlian announces to her callous stepmother (who remains off camera) that she is ready to accept marriage – and then her eyes brim with tears. Her suppressed rage, loneliness and humiliation are to simmer below the surface for the rest of the film.

Songlian arrives at the family compound of her autocratic new husband, Chen (Ma Jingwu), whose face is never clearly seen. This is virtually a walled city-state, subject to Chen’s implacably observed family traditions; Songlian is to be the “fourth mistress” occupying her own quarters, attended to by her own maidservant, the disobedient Yan’er (Kong Lin) who had hoped for “mistress” status herself. There are three other women, each in their own apartment: the stately, impassive “first mistress” Yuru (Jin Shuyuan) of Chen’s own age who has given him a grownup son; the homely, blandly smiling “second mistress” Zhuoyun (Cao Cuifen) who has only managed to give Chen a daughter; and the glamorous, haughty “third mistress” Meishan (He Saifei), a former opera singer who clearly resents Songlian, the new favourite.

Chen presides over it all like a Renaissance Tudor monarch, perhaps deriving unspoken erotic pleasure from capriciously transferring his attentions from one woman to the next. He has a bizarre tradition of putting red lanterns around the apartment of whichever of his mistress-wives he wishes to spend the night with, a decision that is bellowingly announced with elaborate formality by his major domo. (The “first mistress” never gets a red lantern, a mortification she accepts without comment.) And furthermore, the mistress currently enjoying Chen’s favour is allowed a privileged kind of foot-massage from a skilled ancient servant, a kind of quasi-conjugal pleasure.

In this way, Chen’s power and authority are imposed with a mesmeric choreography. For their part, his mistresses have to judge how and by how much to undermine each other without getting into trouble, and also how much to submit or show rebellion to Chen himself. A pouting display of resentment might amuse or arouse the master but, pushed too far, it might result in punishment and a disastrous loss of face. Poor Songlian is left alone for much of the day, and chances across a locked section of the compound where some unhappy mistresses are reputed to have died by hanging some time ago. She at first assumes that these women have taken their own lives, but as things turn out, this might not have exactly been the case. More and more, this dysfunctional household starts to resemble, in modern terms, a kind of death cult.

But it is Chen’s achievement – and in its way, the film’s achievement – to make you accept the normality of what is happening. The deeply strange business with the red lanterns and the foot massage is the culture of this enclosed world, which Songlian and the camera never leave. Songlian is to discover a plot against her, via the slippery and treacherous Yan’er who, as the lower-caste figure, is to pay a higher price than any of them. But the film shows that there are, potentially at any rate, any number of poisonous plots and stratagems swirling around at any moment. Survival is about anticipating them and turning them against one’s enemies without abandoning the mask of sisterly politeness.

This is a thrilling, fascinating study in intimate political savagery and a ruthless competition for the right to exist. The women are pitted against each other and their tragedy is that they do not realise that there is no difference between them; they are all decorative items, preserved, cherished or snuffed out like the red lanterns themselves.

stories.body:
California’s 2026 legislative session has officially adjourned and it’s time to reflect on the wins and losses that have shaped Californians’ digital rights landscape this year. This was the second year of a two-year legislative session, which meant several bills resumed their legislative paths from 2025 .

EFF monitored nearly 100 bills in the state over the two-year session. These included proposed regulations on 3D printers, access to social media platforms, police, commercial, and workplace surveillance practices, AI, and other privacy concerns. While we saw some victories, alarming developments also raised serious concerns about the future of privacy protection in the state.

Celebrating Wins

Use of automated decision-making and surveillance in the workplace

Governor Newsom signed vital protections on the use of automated decision-making in the workplace and workplace surveillance tools, specifically No Robo Bosses ( SB 947 ) and AB 1883 .

Championed by our labor partners , SB 947 limits how employers can use automated decision-making to fire or discipline workers, including provisions that ensure workers get vital information about automated decisions that affect them, and that an algorithm is not the only authority for these consequential decisions. Alongside it, AB 1883 prohibits the use of workplace surveillance to predict emotions or collect neural data. This stops employers from using potentially biased, invasive, and exploitative forms of AI surveillance at the workplace, marking an important step toward creating workplaces that respect the privacy and autonomy of workers. We look forward to continuing to ensure that technology in California’s workplaces is deployed fairly, thoughtfully, and with respect for all workers.

Protecting against federal overreach

EFF was also grateful to see Governor Newsom sign SB 747 , which allows damages lawsuits against federal officials who violate the U.S. Constitution . Victims of constitutional violations deserve a complete remedy and this law also helps deter constitutional violations in the first place. Gaps in current law often make it difficult to seek a damages remedy against federal officials who violate the U.S. Constitution. This bill makes it easier to bring such litigation. Federal law enforcement officials have violated our First Amendment right to record on-duty police and other newsworthy subjects, and also sometimes violate our Fourth Amendment right to be free from unreasonable searches of our phones and laptops . When this happens, the people who suffer these violations should be able to sue these officials for damages .

Additionally, EFF supported two bills (which are now state law) that clarify and extend California’s shield laws to protect patients, healthcare providers, and others involved in reproductive healthcare and gender-affirming care that is legal in California. After the overturn of Roe v. Wade , California enacted numerous shield laws to protect people who provide, receive, or help others obtain healthcare that is legal in California. These laws prohibit California agencies and certain companies from helping other states enforce laws that punish this care. Yet the federal government and coordinated efforts in other states still threaten access to these legally protected healthcare services. AB 1854 addresses these threats by expanding coverage to more California businesses and individuals who receive legal demands, creating a notification process so the Attorney General can intervene to stop improper disclosures, and clarifying that law enforcement cannot arrest someone if the Governor refuses an extradition request. These protections serve as a necessary response to real and escalating tactics outside the state targeting lawful reproductive healthcare.

EFF also supported AB 1930 to protect confidential medical records from politically motivated investigations into lawful healthcare, empowering the California Attorney General’s office to meaningfully intervene and respond to out-of-state subpoenas or requests for data regarding protected care.

Young people online

EFF is dedicated to protecting the rights of young people online. We supported a handful of bills on digital literacy and cybersecurity education that were signed into law, such as AB 2071 on digital wellness instruction and AB 2298 on cybersecurity in educational standards. Unlike blanket bans , these bills address online safety through education rather than prohibition. Young people rely on the internet not just for entertainment, but for civic engagement , education , self-expression , and community —especially vulnerable youth who may lack support in their physical surroundings.

Real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation. Research consistently shows that open, honest conversations about digital literacy and privacy with trusted adults are far more effective at protecting youth than restrictive censorship laws. Young people themselves recognize this need; in fact, AB 2071 was co-authored by a group of students actively seeking better resources to navigate their digital lives safely.

EFF and our allies were also able to stop the expansion of California’s dangerous age gating law from operating systems to browsers. The California legislature stepped back from their plan to expand the 2025 age-gating law and ultimately removed language from AB 1856 that could have compounded serious threats to users’ speech, privacy, and security just to browse the internet, and positively, removed the burdens on open-source operating systems.

Real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation

While EFF still believes the underlying law that AB 1856 amends, AB 1043, is unconstitutional , we appreciate that the legislature did not expand this problematic age-gating framework to browsers. We were also pleased that an earlier amendment to AB 1856 reduced the threat to the open-source community by exempting open-source operating systems. Given these changes, EFF removed its opposition to AB 1856, and thanks the author for listening to concerns from advocates and developers.

Mourning Losses

Updating California’s Information Practices Act (IPA)

EFF was proud to co-sponsor AB 1337 this session alongside our friends at Oakland Privacy and Assemblymember Chris Ward, who is also the chair of the legislative LGBTQ Caucus. The bill unfortunately failed to cross the finish line after stalling in the Senate.

AB 1337 would have updated California's foundational Information Practices Act of 1977 and extended its vital privacy safeguards present at the state agency level to counties and cities. Today, city and county governments collect vast amounts of sensitive personal data (from public health records such as vaccinations, to welfare assistance details, to license plate reader data) and administer programs that were likely not contemplated back in 1977. Yet the law has simply not kept up with modern data practices, and California still has no state law governing how local governments handle this information. While we could not build enough political progress to pass the bill this session, closing this local privacy gap remains an urgent need for California.

Social media ban

Another major setback was the passage (and subsequent signing ) of a social media ban for youth under the age of 16 ( AB 1709 ).

Technology and the laws that regulate it should support and empower young people, but AB 1709 falls far short of this goal. Using technology is how we learn and build community in today’s world, but laws such as AB 1709 cut young people off from essential information and experiences . They also particularly harm those already facing increased challenges who find safety in supportive online communities that they cannot always access in the physical world.

Technology and the laws that regulate it should support and empower young people

Denying minors access to digital forums or stripping out basic tools needed to navigate them will not make young people safer or healthier in the AI age. Research shows social media bans are ineffectual while denying young people opportunities to develop their own voices, share their art, practice religion, or engage in politics. These laws also hurt all of us. Age-gating requirements force everyone to give up more personal information . To verify who can pass through online gates, companies will collect even more data, concentrating power in corporate hands rather than protecting people. AB 1709 is also inconsistent with rights to free expression , meaning California will spend resources defending a law that will likely get tied up in court .

Gutting California’s Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA)

CIPA was originally intended to protect personal privacy against surveillance and included a private right of action so consumers could hold corporations accountable in court. This is why EFF and allied organizations spent the two-year session strongly opposing SB 690 —a bill we dubbed the " Corporate Cover-Up Act " for its attempt to weaken consumer protections in CIPA. Although SB 690 was narrowed from its original draft , we asked Governor Newsom to veto it because it strips away the law's private right of action—a vital tool for individuals fighting back against unlawful metadata surveillance. People deserve the right to decide whether to bring a lawsuit , which remains one of the most effective ways to deter corporate abuse. Unfortunately, the Governor signed the bill and even urged the legislature to go further next year. It's especially alarming to see this disregard for accountability as the federal government and law enforcement agencies seek data from businesses or data brokers to target people based on political beliefs, religious affiliations, or health decisions.

We expect to see further attacks on CIPA next legislative session, as Governor Newsom’s signing statement called for “additional work in this area” and urged the legislature to “take this on next year to ensure a fair balance between protecting private information and preventing rapacious litigation."

Banning the sale of sensitive personal information

California also missed the opportunity to join other states in restricting the sale of sensitive data. We are deeply disappointed that Governor Newsom vetoed AB 1542 , which would have ensured sensitive personal information stays private by banning its sale outright. There's a nationwide movement to protect consumers by making intimate details off-limits for businesses to sell or share. From precise geolocation and genetic data to private messages, health records, sexual orientation, and immigration status, sensitive data reveals the most private aspects of our lives. Monetizing this information fuels financial scams, predatory pricing, and warrant-free government surveillance. By vetoing this bill , California not only fails to lead but falls behind other states, by missing a critical opportunity to protect our most vulnerable communities.

3D printing

The California legislature unfortunately also passed AB 2047 , which aimed to make every 3D printer come pre-loaded with censorship software . It's a law that is trying to prevent an act that is already illegal in the state , and just won't work . It was part of a recent sweep of misguided state bills which purport to go after "ghost guns," but actually “enshittify” 3D printers by introducing privacy risks and a new way to restrict or upcharge users. Lawmakers even considered including misdemeanor charges that would have impacted people using alternative open-source programs. Fortunately an outpouring of opposition from makers and civil liberties advocates resulted in a bill so limited that, despite having passed and been signed into law, will not affect makers until ASTM International publishes a standard — something the organization had not been considering doing .

Where California Missed the Mark

Consumer privacy

California lawmakers also missed key opportunities to curb commercial surveillance. EFF supported AB 2564 , which prohibits retailers from engaging in surveillance pricing , the invasive practice that allows corporations to offer the same product to two different people at two different prices based on scrutiny of their personal data. Unfortunately, the bill stalled on the last day of session.

The legislature also failed to move AB 322 , which would have safeguarded the privacy of Californians by placing restrictions on the collection, use, and sale of location data. Last year, EFF published a rubric for comprehensive location privacy laws , outlining baseline standards states should meet to shield individuals from pervasive location surveillance. Since then, states like Connecticut, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, and Virginia have enacted new consumer privacy restraints on geolocation data . Yet, even as these states move the ball forward, most of their laws leave significant gaps that still must be filled. California failed to make that change and protect residents from location surveillance.

Automatic license plate readers

California lawmakers have lagged in enacting meaningful limits on automated license plate readers with all proposed ALPR regulation bills failing to pass since 2022. SB 1013 initially appeared on track to pass with broad support, but ultimately stalled in the final days of the session.

EFF maintains high standards for ALPR legislation , favoring full bans or, at minimum , strict warrant requirements and brief data retention limits. While we remained neutral on earlier versions of SB 1013, EFF and our partners ultimately opposed the bill after late amendments compromised key privacy protections. The final draft would have doubled the current data retention period and allowed agencies to archive rather than delete data unrelated to active investigations—effectively shifting away from data minimization toward indefinite retention. (We saw San Francisco adopt a similar proposal this year ). We encourage California lawmakers to draw from our ALPR legislative agenda to enact robust safeguards or ban ALPR mass surveillance altogether.

Looking Ahead

Next session, we expect ALPR legislation to be top of mind as states across the country reckon with the harms the technology has caused. We will also be monitoring the results and action following the state’s audit into California’s fusion centers . Following calls from advocates to address privacy abuses and a lack of transparency, the Joint Legislative Audit Committee approved Senator Sabrina Cervantes’ audit request in March 2026. This builds on our past experiences working with JLAC audits to expose law enforcement overreach—such as the state auditor's damning 2020 report on law enforcement’s use of automated license plate readers and our 2016 push to fix the deeply flawed CalGang database . The audit will examine the legal authority, governance, and funding of the centers, map out state and private data systems accessed by personnel, and review protocols for handling data breaches and unauthorized surveillance. This audit will mark the first comprehensive review of these facilities in 13 years and should be released by Summer 2027. We hope lawmakers use the findings to rein in these centers and their unauthorized surveillance.

Other “zombie bills” are also expected to return next year, including legislation regarding the use of copyrighted material to train AI systems. Throughout the two-year session, EFF raised serious concerns about AB 412 , a bill that would require AI developers to identify and disclose copyrighted works used in generative AI training. We argued that complying with such a mandate is practically impossible , as it demands information that often does not exist and cannot realistically be obtained. While we are glad the legislature paused to consider the best approach rather than rushing this policy forward, we expect legislation targeting fair use and AI training to return next session.

More broadly on AI, vulnerabilities and security issues have dominated recent news cycles, and everyday Californians feel real anxiety about the risks of AI. We expect to see numerous bills addressing issues like existential risk and kill switches , as Assembly and Senate privacy committees in California have held informational hearings on these topics over the last month.

We hope to work with legislators to address the threats of AI and ensure that technology supports rights, justice, freedom, and innovation for all people. Laws should always ensure that technology empowers rather than oppresses.

stories.title: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
stories.summary: Job, loans and savings are all affected by the rise in interest rates announced by the Bank of England.

stories.body:
Published 5 November 2026

Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you.

Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you.

1. Jobs and pay

Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level.

Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.

This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up.

Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate.

Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises.

Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.

That could include greater use of robots rather than workers.

"It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said.

"You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further."

2. Boost to savings

The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products.

So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news.

When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too.

The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates.

What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages? Published 1 day ago

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it Published 28 September

Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go? Published 11 hours ago

Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty.

"Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.

She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative.

The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords.

3. Mortgages and loans

The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages.

About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.

Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost is going up by about £31 a month now the Bank has raised the base rate, but it depends on the size of people's loans.

An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) must wait to see if their lender chooses to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.

If you, like 87% of mortgage-holders, have a fixed-rate deal, then the payments will stay the same until the end of your current deal, which is usually two or five years.

While monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, future deals are. Lenders had already "priced in" the latest rate rise when quoting new deals. Expectations for the Bank rate into next year are crucial on what they offer next.

The average rate on fixed deals are much higher now than was predicted at the start of the year. It means those remortgaging, possibly after the post-Covid boom in the housing market, are facing the prospect of higher mortgage payments.

Some people have been choosing to move onto tracker deals instead, taking a view - including some risk - of the Bank rate not moving towards a series of further hikes.

In today’s newsletter: From the cost of living to the AI bubble and the fight against fascism, Weber answers Guardian readers’ questions on how to build a fairer economy and world

G ood morning. As stateside celebrations die down, the Democratic party will be forced to confront a (deceptively) simple question: now what? Their colossal midterm successes will curtail Trump’s power during his remaining time in office, but the battle to shape the Democratic platform heading into next year’s presidential primaries is only just getting started.

While rallying against Trump is one thing, sustaining support by making a tangible difference to the lives of voters struggling with the cost of living is another. It’s a challenge for progressive parties facing down the far right across the world.

For years, economist Isabella Weber has argued that progressive politicians can win back voters by focusing on a fundamental issue: make life’s necessities – housing, transport, food, water, energy, healthcare – affordable to all. It’s the basis of her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics , and her ideas have found a receptive audience in New York, where Zohran Mamdani, who has followed Weber’s work for years, has made affordability central to his agenda. Now, a raft of progressive candidates have won on similar platforms . Weber’s influence is also being felt in the UK, with Andy Burnham’s Labour conference speech echoing much of her messaging.

A few weeks ago, we asked you to send in questions for Weber. In today’s First Edition, she answers them. That’s after this morning’s headlines.

Five big stories

UK | Cocaine has overtaken heroin as the biggest cause of drug deaths in England and Wales, figures from the Office for National Statistics show.

France | Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in demonstrations across France as trade unions call for a nationwide strike expected to extend to hospital workers, air traffic control, the post office, teachers and rail staff.

Commonwealth summit | The UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year with Caribbean nations affected by the slave trade and its legacy, Commonwealth leaders have said.

US news | Pete Hegseth is increasingly looking like he may take the fall for Republicans’ midterm losses, despite Donald Trump’s vocal support for his defense secretary, even calling him a champion of war.

Ebola | A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

Isabella Weber answers your questions

What are the most interesting or radical actions governments are taking to improve affordability in an increasingly volatile world? Jack in Ireland

IW: Mexico’s government has an agreement with grocery companies to fix the price of a basket of essential foods. President Claudia Sheinbaum is making clear that it is her responsibility to negotiate on behalf of ordinary people and make essentials affordable. This is the opposite of neoliberalism, which tells people that democracy is the greatest system, yet that elected officials can do little to meet their basic material needs. Mexico has also capped energy prices, guaranteed small-scale farmers minimum prices for staples to encourage domestic production, and built emergency buffer stocks.

Spain capped the price of gas for power generation, which effectively contained the 2022 energy shock, offered free commuter and regional rail passes while the crisis lasted, and established public scrutiny of corporate profits.

At the municipal level, Vienna stands out : around half of its residents live in municipal or subsidised housing. Istanbul has pioneered people’s canteens that offer nutritious meals at an affordable price point. And New York City has put affordability policies such as rent freezes, investment in housing stock and public supermarkets back on the international agenda.

﹡﹡﹡

How should these midterm results shape Democratic economic policies? Should they be cautious or bold? Jessica in Brighton, UK

The Democrats won votes on affordability , and now they must have the courage to deliver real change. A dignified life for all must be the north star and that requires a fundamental overhaul of the economic playbook. Last time the Democrats enjoyed an electoral wave was in 2008, and under Obama they then leaned into neoliberalism. Bidenomics got stuck in a halfway house.

This time, the economy needs to be rebuilt starting from the essentials – energy, food, housing, communication, transport, all forms of care – with investments that create meaningful and decent jobs. Short term measures such as price policies can buy time and build power to regain public control over the essentials on which our lives and industries depend. We must then change how we provide them so that provision is compatible with planetary boundaries while constraining corporate power.

﹡﹡﹡

Why do governments use interest rates to control inflation? It seems unfair and clumsy. Simon in Perth, Australia and James in Leeds, UK

We often say interest rate hikes cool down the labour market – it sounds nice, like a fresh breeze. But simply put, the goal of rate hikes is to curb inflation by increasing unemployment and weakening workers’ ability to demand high wages. Higher rates also raise the cost of investments, for example in renewable energy that would make our economies less vulnerable to future shocks, and they increase mortgage costs, deepening the housing affordability crisis. This causes considerable harm, potentially pushing people towards the far right.

That is why I argue for surgical, sectoral stabilisation policies for essentials that buy time for structural measures. Rate hikes remain the standard response, whatever the nature of inflation, because central banks are in charge of monetary stability and have only one instrument at their disposal. We need a new approach in which governments fight inflation too, and central banks take on new tasks such as monitoring profit margins and issuing early warnings about rising prices of essentials that can unleash inflation.

﹡﹡﹡

Why do economists accept 2 to 3% inflation as OK but not 0%? Wouldn’t consumers be better off if prices went down rather than up? Rich in Michigan, USA

The 2% target is an arbitrary rule of thumb for central banks, established relatively recently. But the idea that a little inflation supports steady growth is old. If purchasing power slowly declines, there is an incentive to invest or spend rather than hoard cash in your mattress. Moderate inflation also makes debt servicing easier, both for private borrowers and governments.

﹡﹡﹡

Why are we obsessed with economic ‘growth’? It seems to drive self-destructive behaviour. Richard in Hampshire, UK and Tim in Lewes, UK

This is a live debate, especially in the context of climate change. Capitalist economies are predicated on growth because capital always strives for greater profits, but growth does not automatically guarantee a dignified life. What I am arguing for is to replace this growth imperative with an affordability and full- employment imperative: essentials should be removed from profit fundamentalism and organised to ensure affordable provisioning for all, and the government should be responsible for guaranteeing decent and meaningful jobs.

﹡﹡﹡

I support a vigorous tax on wealth. Something like a 100% tax on all wealth over $1 b n. Do you agree? Bill in Virginia, USA

Roosevelt warned that “the liberty of a democracy is not safe if private power grows stronger than the democratic state itself: That, in its essence, is fascism-ownership of government by an individual, by a group, or by any other controlling private power.” This was a key lesson from the consolidation of the Nazis’ power. Taxing the ultra-rich to limit extreme wealth concentration is key to anti-fascist economics. A 100% tax on wealth over $1bn might, however, not be the best design. A progressive tax that limits wealth accumulation starting at somewhat lower levels would make it harder to amass a billion dollars to begin with.

﹡﹡﹡

What will happen if the AI bubble bursts? Fiona in Edinburgh, UK

The immediate impact would probably be a stock market crash and a financial crisis. But such a crisis would also present an opportunity to turn things around. Governments should not bail out the companies but socialise them and turn them into democratically controlled utilities.

AI has cannibalised humanity’s knowledge and automated it to make profits for a handful of companies that openly state their business could lead to human extinction; it should serve the common good instead. As it creeps into our work and we increasingly rely on it in our daily lives, we will have to take public control of AI while also creating space for knowledge creation and creativity that are not competing with AI services. Otherwise, exercising the mind will become a privilege of the wealthy few. Some questions have been condensed for clarity.

What else we’ve been reading

Having recently finished reading Yesteryear, I find myself perhaps more fascinated by trad wives than I’d like to be. Lucy Knight’s deep dive into the women leaving the movement, was excellent and eye opening. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

I love Coco Khan’s writing, so I made a beeline for her column on why celebrities wear tone-deaf Halloween costumes . In it, she unpicks “the strange, insulated life that comes with sustained wealth”, while being very funny and somehow, against all odds, hopeful?! Genius. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

There are so many ways to put together a stunning portrait. I loved looking at this year’s gallery from the Winston Taylor Portrait Prize – call me basic, but my favourite is the six-year-old Elvis impersonator. Poppy

I am not one of those admirable souls who gets their Christmas shopping sorted with weeks to spare. But having realised there’s nothing in this gift guide that someone in my life wouldn’t love, I feel this could be the year I’m done and dusted by mid-November. Lucinda

The front pages

“Trumped”, is the Guardian ’s front page headline today, while the FT goes with “Crushing midterm rebuke to Trump”, and the Times writes “Trump faces backlash as Democrats make history. The Telegraph writes “Vance turns on Trump”, similarly The i Paper has “Vance blames Trump’s war for crushing defeat”, and the Mail says “Maga turns on Trump”. The Mirror ’s headline is “Reborn in the U.S.A.”, and Metro writes “Lame Donald Duck”.

Other high-profile creatives backing the scheme, which invites Londoners to offer spare rooms to writers at reduced rates, include Jack Thorne, who co-created Adolescence, and James Graham, who wrote the stage show Dear England.

stories.title: 'Not my job to set a budget,' says secretary of state
stories.summary: Sir Chris Bryant is understood to have asked parties to commit to raising an extra £200m in income.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget

Published 5 November 2026

The Northern Ireland secretary has said that it is not his "job" to set a budget and that it is the responsibility of the Northern Ireland Executive.

This comes after no resolution was reached in negotiations between executive parties and Sir Chris Bryant.

He is understood to have presented a set of conditions, including revenue raising, to be attached to any potential deal on a Stormont budget.

Sir Chris said: "They really have to take me seriously when I say there is no more money."

Seven months into this financial year the Northern Ireland Executive has still not agreed a budget.

Speaking after a series of one-to-one meetings, the First Minister Michelle O'Neill said there was still "no white smoke".

Democratic Unionist Party leader (DUP) Gavin Robinson said he felt there was a level of optimism that was "not matched by the reality inside" the room during talks.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant (right) greets Finance Minister John O'Dowd at Hillsborough Castle

Speaking on BBC Newsline , Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget.

He described talks ending without agreement as "a bit frustrating" but added that he's still "hopeful".

He said: "I just wanted to get a move on" and added: "Whatever the total envelope is you have to live within it".

Sir Chris also said he would only set a budget for Northern Ireland if the executive parties asked him to.

"They should be able to put together their budget but they have to decide what their priorities are."

The Sinn Féin delegation was made up of Michelle O'Neill, John O'Dowd, Mary Lou McDonald and Caoimhe Archibald

After talks with the secretary of state, the first minister said that while there may be things dividing the executive, her party would persist in trying to get a budget deal done that allows public sector pay awards to be made for this year.

O'Neill also said she was getting "impatient" with the government and that she would take no lectures from it about managing finances.

Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson said the secretary of state is "not moving"

The DUP leader said: "As it stands today, the secretary of state is not moving, the practical, honest reality of that is that without additional resource, there will not be a balanced budget".

Robinson added that "there will be no legal ability to do what it is we think the executive needs to do, and what we want it to do" without a budget.

Bryant says executive should improve 'discipline'

Stormont ministers argue the UK's devolution funding formula no longer delivers enough for them to balance their books.

The government had offered them an additional £525m this year, but they said it still left significant gaps in managing their spending pressures, particularly delivery of pay awards for public sector workers.

It is not clear what the shape of a final budget agreement could look like, with some parties insisting there is still scope to "reprofile" some of the financial package.

Bryant's conditions are believed to include the executive committing to £200m in additional revenue raising in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

He has also asked that they should improve "discipline" around promises and delivery of pay parity to public sector workers in Northern Ireland.

Health Minister Robbie Butler, UUP leader Jon Burrows and Steve Aiken spoke to the media outside Hillsborough

Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows said he did not want to sound "defeatist" and would continue to engage with the government.

But he said there was a real prospect that it would be resolved in time to avert the potential of strike action by health care workers waiting on pay uplifts for this year.

Speaking before talks with the secretary of state, Alliance's Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir said it is now "make your mind up time" for the executive.

"This needs to be resolved not in weeks or months, but days. We need to come to a final conclusion and give certainty to people who deserve proper pay but also in terms of investment in public services we need to get this done," he added.

Speaking on BBC NI's The View programme, Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna said a budget is "an agreement to take responsibility and an agreement to prioritise".

Her party, which is the official opposition in the legislative assembly, is "very clear about the severe constraints," she said, but added: "the fact is by not having a budget in month eight of this financial year, everybody who's trying to operate in that budget is running at 95%".

Where are the budget negotiations at?

Talks between the government and the executive parties have been taking place for several months now , but earlier this week O'Dowd warned that a "crunch point" is approaching.

On Tuesday, the executive met again, with O'Dowd saying afterwards that he planned to present a series of options to his ministerial colleagues in the days ahead about a way forward.

He did not divulge what those may be, but the government has already said no to a request from the executive to allow a larger chunk of the money in the three-year offer to be spent this year, referred to as "front-loading".

What happens in the absence of a budget?

Without an agreed budget, departments face operating on emergency spending restricted to 95% of the prior year, with warnings that funds could run out by January.

The secretary of state has also warned that a cost-of-living £100 payment cannot be made to households in Northern Ireland until an executive budget is agreed .

That came after the government announced its first budget under Andy Burnham last week, with Northern Ireland getting an additional £270m for public services as a result, of which £131m can be used this year.

Sir Chris has said that he is exploring contingency measures to allow him to pass a budget bill at Westminster, in the event that a deal cannot be reached to do so at Stormont.

stories.title: Join EFF to Celebrate the Life of Aaron Swartz
stories.summary: Join us to celebrate the legacy of Aaron Swartz on Nov. 8, 2026. With the organizers of Aaron Swartz Day , we’re honoring his life with an in-person and remote hackathon. This event is supported by several organizations that carry on his work, including the Internet Archive—which is hosting the in-person event—the Freedom of the Press Foundation , Creative Commons and the Free Law Project . Aaron Swartz was a digital rights champion who believed in the need for an open internet. His life was cut short in 2013, after federal prosecutors charged him under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) for systematically downloading academic journal articles from the online database JSTOR. Facing the prospect of a long and unjust sentence, Aaron died by suicide at the age of 26. EFF was proud to call Aaron a friend and ally. We continue to stand with programmers and developers engaged in cutting-edge exploration of technology through our Coders' Rights Project . Hackathon participants can contribute code, documentation, and design to several open-source and public-interest projects. These include Secure Drop , Open Library , Quantifying the Commons , Onion Press , and our own Atlas of Surveillance . EFF Director of State Affairs Hayley Tsukayama will also join hackathon participants at the Internet Archive at 11 a.m. for an Atlas of Surveillance on-boarding session. Contributors across experience levels are welcome. The Aaron Swartz Day organizers are also open to adding new projects and workshops, so please contact them at aaronswartzday@gmail.com if you’d like to suggest a workshop or project—particularly open-source projects on Github that participants can continue to work on after the event. For more details on how to participate in-person or remotely, please visit the Aaron Swartz Day and International Hackathon page at www.aaronswartzday.org . stories.body:
Base rate increases from 3.75% and Bank governor signals another rise in near future to combat rising inflation

Analysis: Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous

The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the rise, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase.

The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices persistently above $100 a barrel in recent months, as hopes have evaporated of a deal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz .

As a result, the Bank now expects UK inflation to rise to 4.9% in the middle of next year – up from 3.2% in its last economic forecast in July. Inflation hit 3.5% in September , as measured on the consumer prices index.

The decision, which will hit mortgage borrowers, comes a week after John Healey used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers. Echoing the Office for Budget Responsibility’s gloomy forecasts for living standards , the MPC expects real post-tax income to fall this year and next.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey , raised the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

“Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach,” he said, according to the MPC minutes.

However, he played down the likelihood of a prolonged series of increases, as markets have been predicting. “Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence in hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase,” he said.

The Bank’s next interest rate decision will be announced on 17 December, and some analysts suggested the MPC could press ahead with a pre-Christmas hike.

Andrew Goodwin, the chief economist at consultancy Oxford Economics , said: “The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike in December or February is likely.”

Explaining its decision to raise borrowing costs, the MPC highlighted the pass-through from elevated oil prices to business and consumer costs across the economy. It expects the Ofgem energy cap to rise from the equivalent of £1,723 a year for an average household in Great Britain to £2,150 in January and to increase again in April. Food price inflation could hit 4.75% by mid-2027, it warned.

Businesses have so far reported in the Bank’s surveys that they have been able to absorb soaring oil and gas prices – by hedging their energy costs, for example – but the MPC believes they will soon have to start passing them on to consumers in higher prices.

It is also concerned about workers seeking to offset the impact of the higher cost of living by asking for bumper pay rises.

after newsletter promotion

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, after the Democrats’ victories in the US Congress, which some investors have interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has blamed the war, and its impact on inflation, for the rout at the polls.

Speaking at the Bank’s press conference, Bailey welcomed the sharp fall in energy prices in the last 48 hours but said it would need to be sustained to change his view about the need for future rate rises. “This is positive news, but there is already a significant amount of inflationary pressure in the pipeline,” he said, adding: “What is the best thing that can happen? It is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East.”

While the decision to increase rates was supported by all MPC members, the minutes of the meeting reveal stark divisions over how much further they may need to go to bring inflation under control. The dovish Alan Taylor suggested this should be a “risk-management ‘one-for-now’ insurance hike”, while Mann argued that an immediate half-point rise was necessary to restore the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility.

Healey’s budget included measures aimed at cushioning the impact of higher energy prices – including extending the fuel duty freeze and the VAT cut on electricity bills. The MPC said the package would shave a quarter percentage point off inflation in mid-2027.

Responding to the interest rate increase, Healey said: “The Iran conflict is reaching deep into the pockets of families and businesses here at home.

“In my budget I acted to give some breathing space to families and businesses. Twenty million households will get a £100 energy payment, I extended the tax cut on electricity bills and froze fuel duty. I also set out the course ahead to get costs down for good.”

But the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, called the rate rise “another headwind for hardworking families to deal with”.

stories.body:
Foreign Office says 10-year sentence shows city’s security law is being used to ‘target individuals for political expression’

Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case

The UK and the US have condemned the 10-year sentence given to Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong under a controversial national security law.

Wong, 30, was sentenced on Thursday after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” under the law. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said that Wong’s sentence was “a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation”.

The spokesperson added: “We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).”

The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.

Shortly after the US consulate strongly condemned the sentence on Thursday, China warned “relevant parties” to “stop making irresponsible remarks” about Hong Kong judicial cases.

Human rights groups and politicians from across the political spectrum also criticised the sentence.

Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The harsh sentence on baseless charges against Joshua Wong is cruel and unjust. Young people promoting social change are an asset for any vibrant society, but the Hong Kong government puts them behind bars.”

Sarah Brooks, deputy regional director for Amnesty International, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”

She said the new conviction “cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction”.

Wong has already spent six years in detention and had been due for release in January 2027.

In the most recent Foreign Office report on Hong Kong, published last month, the UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said that Wong’s case “reinforced concerns about the increasingly broad application of national security legislation”.

Wong’s supporters called on governments around the world to push for his release.

Nathan Law , a Hong Kong activist and friend of Wong’s who was named as a co-conspirator in the case, said: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy.”

Law called the sentencing “a farce” which signified that China “is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil”.

When former British colony Hong Kong was handed to China in 1997, it was promised 50 years of “one country two systems”, under which the city would keep some autonomy and freedoms.

The UK considers Beijing to be in violation of that international treaty, after the crackdown on protests in 2019 and 2020, and the sweeping legal reforms that followed.

Conservative MP Iain Duncan Smith said Wong had “stood up” for that treaty, which he said China had “subsequently trashed”.

He added: “Despite this, the UK government has done little to nothing about it. The more we give in when China breaks the rules, the worse it gets in the future.”

The Labour MP James Naish said: “Hongkongers in my constituency chose Britain for the freedoms Joshua is jailed for defending – values we should all support. This is not a lenient sentence and the government must show China that Britain will not tolerate it.”

stories.title: Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
stories.summary: The goverment argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 hours ago

Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.

The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".

It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.

It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning .

Greater transparency

The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.

Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".

The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union. , external

Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna , external , 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.

Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".

He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".

'More complicated'

Previous research from the CIPD , external , an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.

But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.

CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".

"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."

Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".

The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".

Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".

It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.

At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.

The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.

Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them .

stories.title: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites
stories.summary: Titanium Court is a bizarre world of 8-bit fairies, Shakespeare and surprise songs – its magic lies in never knowing what on earth is going on • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Earlier this year, I was stuck in hospital for several days, fuzzy on pain medication and bored out of my mind, with nothing but a Steam Deck for company. In the middle of one of those long nights, unable to sleep, I played a game called Titanium Court . It’s a strange creation that looks like it was made for the ZX Spectrum and reads like a postmodern Shakespeare adaptation – a compelling mix of strategy game and match-3 where you rearrange battlefields by matching tiles, before sending tiny lo-fi fairy armies to their deaths. At the end of this late-night run, I met a boss I’d defeated before – a comically hungry dragon – and the game asked if I would like to skip the boss fight and enjoy a musical performance instead. A game has never asked me this before. Of course, I accepted. stories.title: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
stories.summary: Markets have been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry following the US midterms.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 November 2026

Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development.

Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.

The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.

In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning.

The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 5% lower in early trading as Panasonic shares lost over 10% and Hitachi slipped by almost 8%.

Major tech companies also drove South Korea's Kospi down by more than 8.5%. Chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 11.5%, while Samsung was down by nearly 10%.

Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the onslaught of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.

They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.

Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.

In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents.

"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said.

"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!"

Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that.

"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.

Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.

Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value.

Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.

Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.

In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.

The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.

The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.

Live: What can Democrats do with control of Congress? We answer your US midterms questions

Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?

Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.

"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.

"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."

Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.

OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.

"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.

Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea.

"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.

Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction .

stories.body:
This year may be seen as a turning point in the climate crisis. The UN has accepted that global warming is going to exceed 1.5°C, while climate scientists have concluded that the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade.

What’s worse, the world may be approaching climate tipping points that could trigger further heating and catastrophic environmental change.

Back in 2018, an international team led by Earth system scientist Will Steffen warned that continued greenhouse gas emissions and destruction of biodiversity could produce a cascade of warming that would culminate in the climate systems passing a threshold into a so-called “ Hothouse Earth ”.

The engine of this cascade would be individual tipping points in the climate. For example, the shutdown of certain Atlantic Ocean currents would not just plunge Europe into freezing winters, but could significantly starve the Amazon rainforest of water vapour. A drought that turns the Amazon to savanna would have huge consequences for the global carbon cycle and climate system. Further warming would accelerate ice sheet loss and ramp up temperatures.

As various tipping points are passed, the Earth system reaches a threshold that could produce a rise in temperatures greater than any for the past 1.2 million years. This would have devastating impacts on ecosystems and societies. Indeed, it’s hard to see how complex, industrialised civilisation would be able to exist in a world that has rapidly warmed beyond 4°C.

Are we responding to the risks?

To what extent the Earth system has the capacity to produce this sort of cascading warming is a topic of intense scientific research . We may be lucky, in that individual tipping elements such as Atlantic current collapse require much higher levels of warming , or more fundamentally the Earth’s current climate may prove to be more resilient than we think. Unfortunately, the opposite may be the case and a planetary threshold may lurk at lower levels of warming than Steffen and colleagues proposed.

It seems reasonable to assume that a deepening climate crisis will focus minds and spur climate action. Unfortunately, new research by my coauthors and I suggests the exact opposite may happen: the worse climate change gets, the harder it could be to stop it. The end point of that process is a disastrous acceleration towards further warming .

Rather than being a purely theoretical exercise, we propose that we can begin to see signs of this slide away from climate action in the real world. For example, those nations most at risk from climate change can be caught in a sovereign debt “doom loop” whereby the damage caused by extreme weather reduces their abilities to repay loans and makes it harder to obtain desperately needed finance to both mitigate and adapt to climate change.

This feedback loop can derail climate policy over time: as debt servicing consumes growing shares of government revenue, climate investments are sidelined, and the country becomes increasingly exposed to climate change.

Increased warming can also increase conflict , thus undermining international cooperation required for mitigation. This is affected by a range of socioeconomic factors, such as inequality and political polarisation.

For example, see the increase in popularity of Spain’s far right-wing and climate-denying Vox party following the devastating Valencia floods of 2024. While the floods were made much more likely because of human-caused climate change, Vox argued that it was left-wing “ideological” environmental policies that made people more vulnerable to the intense rainfall.

The name we give to these dynamics is “ derailment risk ”, the situation where the consequences of climate change makes it harder to deal with the drivers of climate change, and so sustainability efforts end up being derailed.

Planetary stewardship

Given the potentially devastating consequences of a Hothouse Earth, it seems sensible to minimise the chances of it happening as much as possible. To that end, climate and Earth system scientists have argued that active management of this risk is required.

This “planetary stewardship” goes beyond phasing out the burning of fossil fuels to include strengthening forests, peatlands and other natural stores of carbon, along with behavioural changes, technological innovations, new ways of governing, and transforming social values. But derailment risks could undermine the political and social conditions needed to establish any sort of planetary stewardship.

A key concept here is agency – the capacity to produce change. In the original hothouse framework, agency is essentially one way. Humans affect the Earth system by destabilising it. But humans are not simply an external force acting on the Earth system: we are part of it, and our social and political forces can influence its stability and whether the planet slides into a hothouse state.

We argue that the feedback loops pulling us towards derailment can be stronger than those needed to establish planetary stewardship. That’s because collective action can be easier to destroy than build. At a psychological level, bad events affect people more strongly than good events. This is a factor in how trust within a society can be much easier to undermine than create. Increasing climate change impacts could therefore erode the social institutions needed to sustain effective mitigation and adaptation, just when they are most needed.

To respond to this risk we propose a three-stage framework for assessing and managing derailment threats. First, identify and map feedback loops between the human and natural world; second, anticipate disruption and build resilience; third, develop active responsive governance strategies for periods of escalating instability.

Humans are entirely responsible for the climate and ecological crisis, but we also hold the solutions. Maintaining our agency – the ability to put solutions into practice – may prove to be the keystone for all climate policies.

stories.body:
For decades, competing global development models have shaped sub-Saharan Africa’s agricultural landscape. Traditional western donors, such as the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation ( Norad ), have promoted climate-smart agricultural systems such as conservation agriculture , working through non-governmental organisations . Emerging donors, such as China, champion commercial, market-driven models through private-sector contract farming. They tend to focus on high-yielding export cash crops such as cotton.

Zambia is a good place for studying these dynamics. Donor aid remains critical. The country’s agricultural investment needs exceed the financial resources available from government budgets, domestic financial institutions and private investors. In 2024, the government budget allocation to agriculture, fisheries and livestock was ZMW 13.83 billion (US$528 million), which was 7.8% of the national budget. In the same year, the country received US$108 million in international development financing for its agricultural sector.

As food systems and development researchers at the University of Zambia, we set out to examine whether the origin of aid matters to the outcome. Does it influence whether a rural family has enough food to eat, or do local socio-ecological realities and farming practices matter more?

The role of agriculture is hugely important in Zambia. The agricultural sector accounts for 60% of total national employment. About 70% of the population relies on agriculture for its livelihoods, income and household food security.

Our study examined how top-down foreign aid approaches interact with agrarian realities in eastern Zambia. We aimed to disentangle the relative impacts of donor affiliation (Norwegian versus Chinese aid) and farming systems (conservation agriculture versus conventional farming) on household food security. Conservation agriculture is characterised by minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, and crop rotations that include legumes. Conventional agriculture involves ploughing or ridging and may focus on growing a single crop in the same field for a long time.

Our research produced four main findings:

localised farming practices drive household food security and resilience, far outweighing donor identity

conservation agriculture achieves better food security outcomes than conventional agriculture

low crop diversity makes farmers vulnerable

food insecurity remained deeply structural, affecting women-headed households most.

We concluded from our findings that sustainable agrarian transitions require interventions that address systemic inequalities, particularly in relation to women, and empower locally adapted, ecologically diverse farming systems such as mixed farming systems.

Local farming practices outweigh donor identity

For our study we surveyed over 545 smallholder households in Chipata and Mambwe districts. Eastern Zambia has a variety of climate regions, and both models – the Norwegian-backed conservation projects and Chinese-backed contract farming – operate there.

Read more: Are Chinese investors grabbing Zambian land? Study finds that’s a myth

We started studying the projects in 2014, as part of a project examining donor aid effectiveness in Zambia and Malawi, and continued engaging with the question over the years. We asked farmers about their farming practices, their households, and their food security. In these communities, men are seen as the primary landowners and household heads. About half the households reported that they had not had enough food in the past 12 months.

We report four key findings.

Local farming systems override donor identity

After controlling for farming practices and geographic context, we found that donor affiliation made little difference to food security outcomes. Smallholder conservation agriculture improved food security outcomes by minimising climate risk and increasing crop yields. In contrast, donor aid projects tend to focus on predefined goals that rarely account for local environmental and socio-cultural conditions.

Conservation agriculture drives resilience

Farmers who adopted conservation agriculture achieved better food security outcomes than those using conventional agriculture. Conservation agriculture households consumed a broader range of foods from different food groups, such as carbohydrates, animal proteins, plant proteins, dairy, vegetables and fruits.

Conservation agriculture also proved vital for bridging the lean season . This is the period before harvest, between December and March, when farming households run out of grains from the previous harvest. Where farmers got help to prepare land earlier, they also harvested earlier (nine days before conventional farmers).

Export monocultures are risky

Donors that wanted commercial outcomes created new vulnerabilities. Chinese-backed initiatives, focused primarily on cotton contract farming, provided input loans in exchange for exclusive crop sales. While this model created market opportunities, it also reduced crop diversity. Households under Chinese-backed projects cultivated an average of 2.98 crops, compared with 3.63 under Norwegian-backed programmes that emphasised crop diversification. In drought-prone areas, tying farmers to a single export crop without supporting food crops or agroforestry stripped households of their traditional ecological safety nets.

Structural inequities and blind spots remain

Across all sample groups, female-headed households recorded lower dietary diversity and held fewer assets such as fruit trees and livestock. Cultural norms and patriarchal land tenure systems restrict women’s access to fertile land, extension services and agricultural labour.

When female farmers adopted conservation agriculture despite these barriers, their self-reported food security improved.

Neither Norwegian nor Chinese projects made livestock husbandry part of their interventions. Their models ignored a vital part of local mixed-farming systems that provides animal protein, organic manure, draught power and alternative income during crop failures. Mixed farming systems are more resilient in this region, where dependence on rain-fed agriculture is the norm.

Rethinking aid

Our study identified three strategies that could improve the effectiveness of donor aid in building rural resilience. Development partners and policymakers can:

support crop diversification, soil conservation and agroforestry rather than single export cash crops

explicitly address women’s access to secure land tenure, extension services and labour-saving tools

integrate livestock husbandry into aid portfolios alongside crop production.

Read more: Direct support to small scale farmers reduces poverty – what Zambia is doing right

Overall, international development agencies must move away from rigid, top-down blueprints. Simply changing a donor’s flag or rebranding an aid programme does not inherently improve smallholder livelihoods. Real change requires funding flexible, farmer-led initiatives tailored to local socio-ecological realities.

stories.title: Missouri Voters Just Made It Much Harder for Lawmakers to Overturn Citizen-Led Initiatives
stories.summary: The post Missouri Voters Just Made It Much Harder for Lawmakers to Overturn Citizen-Led Initiatives appeared first on ProPublica .
