stories.imageAlt: A room full of people cheer, clap and wave their hands in the air.
stories.body:
For years, Missouri Republicans worked to undo or restrict voter-approved laws and amendments. In passing Amendment 6, voters have not only protected the ballot initiative process but also dramatically strengthened their power over the legislature.

Across the country on Tuesday, voters delivered a wave of Democratic victories, flipping seats in Congress as well as state legislatures, and weakening a number of Republican majorities.

Missouri was no exception. Democrats made significant gains in the state House, picking up 16 seats, though Republicans still hold every statewide office and maintain control of the legislature.

Nonetheless, the election was more than just a rebuke of President Donald Trump. It reflected a long-simmering frustration with Missouri politicians who, time and again, have sought to override the will of voters — a practice that has intensified under years of Republican control. What’s more, voters went beyond weakening the Republican majority. They approved a constitutional amendment that curtailed the powers of the legislature and shifted more authority directly to the people.

Amendment 6, approved by a decisive margin, sharply limits the legislature’s ability to overturn laws and constitutional amendments enacted through citizen initiatives, and its ability to revive laws voters rejected through referendums.

Missouri Republicans have only themselves to blame, according to political observers who have watched the conflict between lawmakers and voters intensify. They resisted a voter-approved Medicaid expansion, repealed paid sick leave protections and sought to reverse abortion rights. They sometimes packaged their efforts with unrelated culture-war provisions, like limiting healthcare for transgender minors, that were intended to appeal to conservative voters.

Then they tried to persuade voters this summer to surrender some of their own power by changing the constitution to make it harder to pass initiatives in the first place. Voters rejected that proposal by more than a 4-to-1 margin .

“I think the people of Missouri are trying to wrest control back from our legislature because our legislature at this point does not seem to really be representing the majority view in the state,” said Jayne Woods, a professor at the University of Missouri law school who has written about the tension between direct democracy and legislative power.

Benjamin Singer is the co-founder and executive director of the Respect Missouri Voters campaign, which helped organize the push for Amendment 6. He said the frustration stretched back decades, including periods when Democrats controlled the legislature. He said when the campaign began organizing in late 2024, many volunteers were still angry about lawmakers’ decision in 2011 to weaken restrictions on puppy mills that voters had approved just a year earlier.

The campaign, he said, had already built a substantial volunteer operation before Republican lawmakers moved in 2025 to undo voter-approved measures that were intended to mandate paid sick leave and protect abortion rights. Respect Missouri Voters ultimately gathered enough signatures to put Amendment 6 on the ballot, seeking not only to protect the initiative process but to strengthen the electorate’s power over the legislature.

With the passage of that amendment, lawmakers now must get 80% support in both the House and Senate before they can propose changing or repealing measures enacted through citizen initiatives, or move to revive laws voters rejected through referendums. Even then, voters must approve any change in a statewide election. The restriction applies to measures voters have approved since 2010, including the constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights that voters approved in 2024.

Republican lawmakers put a measure on Tuesday’s ballot to restore abortion restrictions , but voters rejected that, too . With the passage of Amendment 6, abortion opponents don’t have a clear path to try again.

Amendment 6 also strengthens the referendum process. In addition to restricting lawmakers’ ability to reenact laws similar to those voters have rejected, the amendment explicitly protects the right of citizens to enact laws and constitutional amendments with a simple statewide majority, rejecting the higher threshold Republican lawmakers had sought to impose earlier this year. And it safeguards the power of Missouri’s courts to rewrite misleading ballot language, a power that Republican officials have repeatedly tried to strip away.

The result, political observers said, could make the legislature less consequential than it once was. Republicans still have the votes to pass most laws, but when voters reject those laws at the ballot box or enact their own measures or constitutional amendments through citizen initiatives, lawmakers will now face significant obstacles to overriding them.

Denny Hoskins, the secretary of state and one of Amendment 6’s most prominent Republican opponents, acknowledged how profoundly it would change the balance of power. Before the election, he told the Missouri Independent that if the amendment passed, “it will basically cut our legislature off at the knees as far as being able to pass laws to reduce crime and cut taxes.”

In text messages on Wednesday, Hoskins said that Amendment 6 weakens the legislature and governor “regardless of party” and predicted that it would be challenged in court. He said that “giving power back to the people” might be a great slogan but that the amendment’s sponsors “have no idea what this actually will do.”

Hoskins himself had tried to keep Amendment 6 off the ballot. In August, he refused to certify the initiative petition, arguing that it violated constitutional restrictions on ballot measures. He also rejected a separate petition seeking a statewide referendum on a newly gerrymandered congressional map that Republican lawmakers, working at Trump’s behest, had approved to give their party another seat in Congress.

The Missouri Supreme Court overruled him in both cases, ordering that the measures appear on the ballot. The court found Hoskins in contempt when he sought to use the map in spite of its ruling. Hoskins backed down and the justices did not have him arrested.

On Tuesday, voters rejected the map too. With Amendment 6 now in place — and Democrats significantly bolstering their numbers in the House — Republican lawmakers aren’t likely to gather enough support to override the voters’ rejection of their map.

Travis Crum, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis and an expert on voting rights and election law, said he knew of no other state with a restriction quite like Missouri’s 80% threshold. But he said the amendment was understandable given the legislature’s repeated attempts to reverse voter-approved policies and its unsuccessful effort this summer to make citizen initiatives harder to pass.

“I think that there’s just been this boiling frustration with how the legislature has ignored the initiative process and then sort of tried to rewrite it to its own ends,” he said.

John Hancock, a former Missouri Republican Party chair and longtime GOP consultant, acknowledged that Republican lawmakers had brought some of the backlash on themselves. But he warned that Amendment 6 could make Missouri a magnet for well-financed out-of-state interest groups seeking to enact laws through ballot initiatives — possibly on taxation or gun policy.

That concern about wealthy outside interests was also central to the Republican-backed proposal to restrict citizen initiatives that voters rejected in August. Gov. Mike Kehoe had spent months warning voters about out-of-state special interests trying to rewrite the state constitution, even while a campaign supporting his proposal to phase out the state income tax benefited from funding from a Delaware nonprofit with undisclosed donors.

Woods said the defeat suggested voters weren’t persuaded by that argument. Regardless of who finances an initiative campaign, she noted, Missourians are the ones organizing, gathering support and ultimately deciding whether to approve the measures.

“I think that the people of the state pretty resoundingly said, ‘No, we don’t believe that that’s true,’” Woods said. “‘We believe this is our citizens who are doing this. This is what we want as citizens.’”

stories.title: Trump’s State Department Is Giving $1 Million to Controversial Group to Study Crimes Against White South Africans
stories.summary: The post Trump’s State Department Is Giving $1 Million to Controversial Group to Study Crimes Against White South Africans appeared first on ProPublica .

stories.imageAlt: A woman is surrounded by children of different ages. A young girl to the woman’s left holds a small American flag in her hand and looks directly at the camera.
stories.body:
The End of Aid

The new award, the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause, comes after it cut human rights funding to nations in crisis. One former diplomat called the move “offensive.”

After slashing funding for programs that documented atrocities and protected human rights abroad, President Donald Trump’s State Department is now granting one of its first new human rights awards to a controversial South African organization that promotes the disputed notion that white farmers are a violently targeted, persecuted group, according to multiple sources knowledgeable about the funding.

The group expected to receive the nearly $1 million award, AfriForum, is a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners, a subset of South Africa’s white population. The organization says its members, who have a “ God-given calling ,” fight for Afrikaner interests and self-governance. The money will be used to “ document hateful rhetoric and violent acts ” against Afrikaners and other minority populations in the country.

The new award comes from a State Department bureau tasked with promoting democracy and human rights internationally. Until last year, those funds were mainly spent in poor and authoritarian nations — to fight corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, or combat child exploitation and sexual abuse in Afghanistan. Since Trump returned to office, his appointees have transformed the bureau, gutting its staff, canceling programs and reorienting some of its funding toward conservative causes in Europe.

Samuel Samson, who was appointed as a deputy assistant secretary to the State Department bureau by Trump, has claimed the U.S. has a “civilizational” connection to Afrikaners, who descend primarily from Dutch migrants and predominantly speak Afrikaans. Samson, who has met with far-right leaders in Europe since joining the administration last year, has framed the U.S. government’s financial support for Afrikaners as grounded in “a common heritage, a common culture, a common way of life, shared history and ultimately a common anthropology.”

Samuel Samson Speaks at Lex Libertas Event

There’s a long shared political history between Afrikaner groups and white nationalists in the U.S., said Audie Klotz, a political science professor at Syracuse University who has studied those connections. But, she said, “There’s no heritage connection here. It’s pure scientific racism. In the history of U.S. immigration, there’s no direct connection between South Africa and the United States.”

AfriForum met with the Trump administration in February 2025 to plead for help. The group told officials that Afrikaners are subject to racial discrimination and murders that are more frequent and asked the administration to “act strongly against hate speech that incites violence” against them, according to a statement .

South Africa is plagued by high rates of violence, and some Afrikaners have been tortured and murdered. But independent researchers have found those killings represent a tiny fraction of murders across the country, whose victims are disproportionately people living in poor urban areas, where residents are predominantly Black. Official government statistics , and two formal inquiries into the matter, do not reveal a pattern of targeted violence against Afrikaners.

But Trump subscribes to the idea that white farmers face a “genocide” and has cited disproportionate violence against them as a reason for punishing Africa’s wealthiest nation. In February 2025, he issued an executive order that cut off hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to South Africa and welcomed Afrikaners to the U.S. as refugees. Since then, the administration has opened the doors to more than 16,000 white South Africans while halting virtually all other immigration. Officials recently told Congress they plan to invite as many as 17,500 Afrikaner refugees to the U.S. in 2027.

AfriForum did not respond to specific questions for this story but said that “our understanding is that the allocation has not yet been finalised. Should the allocation indeed be awarded to AfriForum, we will make a public announcement in this regard.”

The new award is the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause. The white South African group governed the nation for decades under a brutal system of segregation known as apartheid, which kept the Black majority an impoverished underclass until the system was dismantled in 1994. Now, with Black South Africans governing the country, white people — of which Afrikaners are the majority — remain one of the wealthiest segments of the population.

The support has caused dismay among several former high-level diplomats, who spoke to ProPublica anonymously because they fear retribution from the administration.

Two former senior U.S. officials responsible for Africa policy said that they would never have met with AfriForum, let alone funded the group, because it was considered to be politically extreme and not credible. They described the organization as cherry-picking crime statistics to create a misleading narrative. “We would certainly not have funded what we would see as a racially incendiary initiative,” said one of the officials.

The decision to direct money toward the group comes after the Trump administration halted programs that advocated for the end of violence in African countries such as Sudan, where the Biden administration determined in 2025 that there was a genocide , calling it “the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe.”

“It’s offensive to provide funding solely to this one group after we’ve cut off funding in countries undergoing real documented crises,” said David Jandura, who managed the Africa portfolio for the State Department’s human rights bureau for several years and lost his job during the mass layoffs in 2025.

Congress has also raised questions about how the award was made. A Senate aide to Democrats told ProPublica that despite repeated requests to State Department officials, they had not received a briefing outlining the recipients of funds earmarked for democracy and human rights, which they described as “highly unusual.”

“The Trump Administration proceeded with funding fringe right-wing causes internationally despite objections from Congress,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a New Hampshire Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, who described the lack of transparency as “unacceptable.”

In response to a series of questions about the AfriForum funding, a senior State Department official wrote in an email that the department does not comment on funding deliberations and that they routinely keep Congress informed of their actions, consulting extensively on this year’s programming. “The Administration has been clear about its concern about the abhorrent race-based discrimination and violence in South Africa,” the unnamed official wrote. “Human rights protections do not depend on a person’s income or ethnicity.”

In July, ProPublica revealed that the State Department originally intended to give the $1 million research award to Lex Libertas, a small organization founded last year by a former AfriForum executive named Ernst Roets. Trump officials later expanded the potential awardees to a small pool of handpicked organizations. The plan drew outrage from Congress over the content of the award as well as plans to bypass the typical competitive bidding process. After ProPublica’s reporting, the State Department released an open call for the funding opportunity , offering $986,500 to a nonprofit organization to “create a comprehensive record of violence affecting Afrikaner and other South African minority populations.” It’s this grant that is now being awarded to AfriForum.

Both AfriForum and Lex Libertas advocate for Afrikaner rights and have developed relationships with the Trump administration. Trump’s ambassador to South Africa, L. Brent Bozell III, visited AfriForum’s headquarters in September, praising the organization for its neighborhood watch programs while criticizing the South African government for not enacting policies requested by the Trump administration. AfriForum has also met with Trump officials in Washington, D.C. , drawing public criticism from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. And in September, Roets met with administration officials.

AfriForum was founded 20 years ago and, with some 300,000 members, claims to be the biggest civil rights organization in South Africa. It says it aims to “establish self-dependence and growing self-governance” and provides some local civic services, such as garbage collection and systems for reporting pot holes and broken traffic lights . The group has said it distances itself from “white supremacist and extremist groups” and that it disagrees with Trump’s assertion that white South African farmers are experiencing a “white genocide.” But it has also said the South African government is “ targeting the continued existence of Afrikaners ” through racial legislation and the downplaying of farm murders, among other things. Academics and former U.S. diplomats have repudiated some of the ideas the group promotes as racist.

It unsuccessfully challenged a ban on the “gratuitous display” of the national flag flown during apartheid, which a South African court has found to be a form of hate speech. And while the group’s leader, Kallie Kriel, has said apartheid “ was wrong ,” he has also said it did not constitute “ a crime against humanity ” as the U.N. has determined , on the grounds that not enough people were killed during that time.

AfriForum has been focusing on farm attacks since at least 2009. In 2018, during Trump’s first presidency, Kriel and Roets, who was then his deputy, met with government officials in Washington, D.C., about the issue, and Roets spoke about it with Tucker Carlson on Fox News , as the chyron below him announced in all caps, “White farmers brutally murdered every week in SouthAfrica.”

Additional research on crimes against white South Africans is an unnecessary and confusing use of U.S. taxpayer dollars, said Carolyn Holmes, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who studies democracy in southern Africa. Holmes noted that AfriForum already produces annual reports on crimes against farming communities. “These data already exist,” she said. “You don’t need a new study. You don’t even need a far-right study, we have those.”

The U.S. support offers more than a financial boost to the organization. “For some time, AfriForum has been campaigning for recognition of their claim that white people face discrimination and persecution,” said Alex Dyzenhaus, a lecturer in international relations and African politics at the University of St. Andrews. “Before, they were only getting the Tucker Carlsons and the far right of the news ecosystem. Now they have the U.S. government on their side.”

The Trump administration has made the plight of white, rural South Africans a key foreign policy issue. In addition to the early executive order, Trump held a contentious meeting with Ramaphosa in the White House last year where Trump claimed white farmers were being executed. The administration has also considered an ad campaign focused on encouraging more Afrikaners to come to the U.S.

In September, Roets of Lex Libertas met with the White House to discuss what he sees as the crisis facing the Afrikaner community and, along with the New York Young Republican Club, placed 3,000 white crosses on the National Mall to commemorate South African farm murders.

Roets declined to answer specific questions from ProPublica but, in a text message, described the murders of several Afrikaners that he knew personally. He also wrote, “I see the suffering of black people in South Africa, I am deeply moved by it, and I spend every day of my life campaigning to make things better for us all.”

Appearing at a press conference for the Lex Libertas event, Samson, the State Department official, showcased the sharp shift the administration has made in U.S. relations with South Africa. While apartheid has been understood globally as a symbol of racist oppression, Samson described the current South African government as having discriminatory “race-based” policies and a cautionary tale for the rest of the world.

At the end of apartheid, in 1994, South Africa was a “flourishing, prosperous society,” Samson said. Since then, the country has gone to “ruin.” He blamed the fall on a “radical ideological leftist movement that wears human rights, that wears tolerance and inclusivity, as a skin suit to advance their Marxist communist worldview.”

Part of the Trump administration’s solution to this perceived crisis, he said, was to provide the research funding.

stories.title: How This Year's Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger
stories.summary: A monster El Niño is nearing its peak, deepening drought in many parts of the world. Coming as countries slash foreign aid and war chokes supplies of energy and fertilizer, the climate phenomenon could leave millions more people in vulnerable countries without enough to eat. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Dried up rice fields in West Java, Indonesia, where El Niño is fueling an extended drought. Ali Lutfi / NurPhoto via Getty Images

A monster El Niño is nearing its peak, deepening drought in many parts of the world. Coming as countries slash foreign aid and war chokes supplies of energy and fertilizer, the climate phenomenon could leave millions more people in vulnerable countries without enough to eat.

By Nicola Jones • November 5, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.

The impacts of an El Niño can be far reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.

This year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.

Global food prices have been trending upwards for 20 years, thanks to climate change. This year brings additional strains.

“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.” The El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas — including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa — and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.

Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.

Children are treated for malnutrition in Ifotaka, Madagascar. Drought, fueled by El Niño, is expected to worsen food shortages. Razafindrakoto Mamy Nirina / AFP via Getty Images

Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, says Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”

And the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, says Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked, and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched: The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.

As of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees C — breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees C — and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees C, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he says. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.

In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock.

Unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested — though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather says.

All these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” says Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed. Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.

While any year brings its own spates of bad weather — some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change — plenty of events this year have been attributed to the El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the Peruvian anchovy fishery, which was closed dramatically early this year to give anchovies a fighting chance in the face of warm waters and less plankton, one of their main food sources. This industry, typically worth between $2 billion and $3 billion, is a huge contributor to global feed for livestock and aquaculture. As of September, global fishmeal output was about half what it was the year before; fishmeal prices have spiked, with some European salmon farmers turning to cheaper chicken byproducts.

Farmer Darwin Cruz in Los Piches, Honduras, where animals are dying amid one of the worst droughts in decades. Orlando Sierra / AFP via Getty Images

In Indonesia, palm oil mills stopped buying fruit from farmers because an ongoing drought shriveled the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River. In Cambodia, a delayed rainy season is drying out rice fields. Panama has declared a national state of emergency (as it did for the 2023 and 2015 El Niños), and the Panama Canal is carrying less ship traffic and transporting less food in the face of dwindling rainfall. In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock from March to August next year. El Niño-induced drought alongside record summer temperatures in Central America has eaten away at crop yields and threatens that region’s second planting cycle: The E.U.’s Joint Research Centre projects an 83 percent spike in people suffering from acute food insecurity in that area.

Perhaps surprisingly, the global food production outlook for this growing season isn’t as bad as one might think: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) notes that the USDA projects worldwide production of maize, wheat, and rice for 2026-2027 to be just 2.7 percent below the previous year’s production, which will still make it the second largest annual crop on record. “Globally, food supply is not of high concern,” says FEWS NET advisor Amy Ostrander. “The concerns are production changes in some specific regions, such as Southern Africa, and food access.” Even if sufficient crops are harvested in those regions, in other words, some food won’t make it to market and some people won’t be able to afford it.

An analysis by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization concludes that the highest risks from El Niño-prompted droughts will be in the Sahel, Southern Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and in Central America’s Dry Corridor and the Caribbean.

While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says a climate scientist.

One good thing about an El Niño is that meteorologists can see it coming almost a year in advance, unlike freak weather events, which are harder to forecast. This gives agencies a fighting chance to protect people by distributing drought-resistant seeds, for example, securing deals for future emergency food supplies and transport, or setting up income assistance for struggling farmers.

The World Food Programme first tested its forecast-based financing program in Zimbabwe during the 2015 El Niño: Delivering cash to families in one district facing drought helped them to sustain their quantity and quality of food, while a neighboring district that didn’t receive cash aid saw a massive drop. This year, the WFP has been delivering cash and other assistance, including, for example, more than 3,000 airtight silos for farmers in Guatemala to help them safely store grain. As of October, the program says it has reached 28 million people across 15 countries with early warning information and assistance.

Cash is strapped for such programs, though. Funds for global aid were down 30 percent in 2025 from their 2022 peak and are still falling, making it hard for the WFP and others to do their work. In Somalia, the WFP helped 10 million people during a drought in 2022; today, in the face of similar conditions, says Choularton, they can afford to reach less than a million.

El Niño is fueling both droughts and floods, leaving vulnerable countries at risk of food shortages. Sources: Food and Agriculture Organization / World Food Programme / Columbia Climate School. Yale Environment 360 / Made with Flourish

Advanced warning is good, says Lobell, but challenges will still abound, and even harder times may lie ahead as El Niños pile on top of climate change. The peaks of strong El Niños are almost always followed by record-breaking years for the global average temperature. The anomalously hot years of 1998, 2016, and 2024 (the current record holder) all followed hot on the heels of El Niño peaks the year before. While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says Hausfather.

Global warming, of course, also has impacts on food supply. Last year, Lobell published a paper showing that total wheat, barley, maize, rice, and soybean yields are now altogether about 5 percent lower overall than they would have been in a world without climate change. “To a lot of people that sounds like a small number. But the kind of shocks that we talk about can be far smaller than that,” he says. “It doesn’t take much of a supply shift to have an important effect on people’s lives.”

Because the specific places that get warmer and drier during El Niños are different from the specific places that get warmer and drier from climate change, researchers caution that what we see in 2026 won’t be a precise forerunner of things to come. But how we deal with this temporary challenge does say something about the resilience of our food systems, says Lobell, and it will reveal how we might cope in the future with other climate disruptions to crops. “That’s one of the big questions,” he says. “How much can you adapt when the conditions are bad?”

stories.body:
The ambition of the 21st century should no longer be to maximize growth, but to maximize prosperity.

Philipp Humm is an artist, author and ex-tech CEO living in Milan.

More than 2,000 years ago, Aristotle formulated one of history’s most remarkable thought experiments. What, he asked, would happen if tools could obey commands, even anticipate them? What would happen if they could carry out their work entirely on their own?

“If every instrument could accomplish its own work, obeying or anticipating the will of others,” he wrote in “Politics” around 350 B.C.E., “if the shuttle would weave and the plectrum touch the lyre without a hand to guide them, chief workmen would not need servants, nor masters slaves.”

For centuries, this passage was understood primarily as a philosophical allegory. Today, what is striking is not Aristotle’s technical imagination but his political imagination. He was more interested in the social consequences of self-operating machines than in their feasibility.

Artificial intelligence forces us to confront this issue anew: What becomes of a society whose economy, purpose and welfare state are built on wage labor if wage labor loses that foundational role? Perhaps the true AI revolution will begin in our conception of what it means to be human, not inside Silicon Valley’s data centers.

More Or Less?

What’s better: more people or less work for humans? Few contradictions capture our historical moment more precisely. Never before has a society simultaneously spent so much money attempting to compensate for labor shortages while investing so much in technologies designed to eliminate labor altogether.

If current fertility rates continue and net migration falls to zero, United Nations projections suggest that many Western populations will shrink by about 30% by the end of this century. In countries such as Italy, the decline approaches 40%-50%. Governments have responded with generous family subsidies and large-scale immigration programs but have seen limited economic success. Research suggests that immigration’s fiscal contribution depends heavily on education, employment, age at arrival and migration motive. Highly skilled migrants, the minority, tend to generate net economic gains, whereas low-skilled immigration, the majority, can impose a net fiscal drag on advanced welfare states.

In Britain, falling fertility, population aging and migration have become inseparable topics. Parliamentary debates frequently frame birth rates as a long-term growth problem. At the same time, the government seeks to reduce reliance on migrant labor by expanding domestic training programs. In the United States, similar arguments are made from the opposite side: Economists warn that the native-born labor force is shrinking and that immigration now supplies much of America’s labor-force growth. Also, a new Silicon Valley pronatalism has emerged. Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and other technology leaders warn that collapsing birth rates threaten civilization, even as their companies build systems designed to reduce the economy’s dependence on human labor.

In addition to trying to stabilize the size of their labor force, governments invest aggressively in artificial intelligence to stay internationally competitive. The labor displacement that these technologies will ultimately produce is often ignored or dismissed with reassuring promises that new jobs will inevitably emerge, as they always have in the past.

“Perhaps the true AI revolution will begin in our conception of what it means to be human.”

The management of this contradiction is even more striking in East Asia.

South Korea, with a fertility rate of around 0.75 children per woman, is experiencing a demographic collapse unprecedented in peacetime. The government spends tens of billions each year on birth and family incentives and housing programs designed to reverse the trend. So far, little success. Simultaneously, South Korea has become the most robot-intensive economy in the world with over 1,000 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers.

Japan presents a similar picture. Its working-age population has been declining for more than two decades, and the country has responded by pursuing one of the world’s most ambitious automation and robotics strategies. Today, Japan possesses one of the highest densities of industrial robots with more than 400 per 10,000 manufacturing workers, compared to the world average of around 120-150.

South Korea and Japan offer a preview of the intelligence economy. Their governments are investing in automation to compensate for shrinking workforces while trying to arrest population decline to preserve domestic demand and the fiscal foundations of their welfare states. Both policies make sense within the industrial economy. But what happens when AI and robotics reduce the economy’s dependence on human labor? Could demographic decline and automation eventually become complementary rather than opposing forces?

The Invention Of Homo Faber

The labor society as we know it today is not an anthropological constant. For most of human history, people were not primarily Homo faber — the productive individual who derives social worth from economic work. They became so only with the rise of modernity, and above all through the Industrial Revolution.

In classical antiquity and most of medieval Europe, manual labor was regarded as a necessity performed largely by slaves and the lower classes. The privileged classes devoted themselves to politics, philosophy, religion, war, arts and leisure. As Hannah Arendt observed in “The Human Condition” (1958), modernity radically overturned the classical hierarchy of human activities. Labor, once regarded as a necessity of life rather than its purpose, increasingly became the organizing principle of society.

Adam Smith provided the intellectual economic foundation for this transformation. In “The Wealth of Nations” (1776), he argued that the true wealth of a nation lies in the total productive labor of its people, not in gold, land or trade surpluses.

Around 1800, roughly 75% of Americans worked in agriculture. Today, fewer than 2% do. America’s industrial transformation created an entirely new economic logic, one symbolized by Henry Ford’s famous wage increase in 1914. Ford understood that his workers should build automobiles and earn enough to buy them. That insight captured the genius of industrial capitalism: production, wages and demand were bound together.

“If artificial intelligence assumes an increasing share of productive labor, society will have to find answers to how to cultivate lives that remain meaningful outside employment.”

This model was at the core of Western democracies throughout the 20th century. Wages financed taxation, welfare systems and pensions. At the same time, they generated income that sustained consumption and served as the principal mechanism of social integration. In numbers, labor accounts for up to 60% of GDP and private consumption for nearly 70% for OECD nations.

The importance of wages extends far beyond the hours people spend at work. Every productive hour finances about nine hours of non-working life: the years of childhood, education and retirement; evenings, weekends and illnesses. Another way to look at it is that every hour of paid work supports those hours of non-working life across society, including workers’ own time outside employment and that of children, students, retirees, homemakers and other dependents. Historically, these ratios have increased, driven mainly by reductions in working hours and increases in life expectancies.

When jobs become scarcer or wages lose their economic bargaining power, this architecture begins to fracture. This puts immense pressure on public finances: Children, retirees, students, the sick and much of public spending ultimately depend on the wages of the working population.

The defining economic problem of our century so far has been How does a society finance ever more years of life with ever fewer years of work? For decades, advanced economies have managed to answer that question through a fragile combination of economic growth and rising public debt. But what happens when artificial intelligence begins to undermine the labor market on which that answer rests?

When Intelligence Becomes Cheap

Every major technological revolution transformed a scarce factor of production into an abundant one. The Industrial Revolution dramatically reduced the cost of mechanical energy with fossil fuels. Globalization in the 1990s and 2000s lowered the cost of physical labor by integrating China and other emerging economies into global production networks. The AI revolution may now do the same with intelligence. Cognition, coordination, pattern recognition and many forms of decision-making could become abundant rather than scarce resources.

John Maynard Keynes anticipated this possibility almost a century ago. In his 1930 essay “Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren,” he warned of what he called technological unemployment: the possibility that humanity might discover ways of saving labor faster than it could discover new uses for it.

For decades, economists largely dismissed this concern in two ways. The first was Joseph Schumpeter’s theory of creative destruction. Technological progress destroys existing occupations, but it also creates new industries, new professions and ultimately more productive forms of employment. The second was historical experience. Every previous technological revolution had ultimately generated more people employed, not mass unemployment.

With AI, this historical adjustment mechanism may no longer be applicable.

The Stanford economist Erik Brynjolfsson has described this possibility as the “Turing Trap.” Previous generations of machines primarily replaced physical labor in a few defined routines. Human beings remained one step above the machines, becoming their planners or problem-solvers. That historical shock absorber is now shrinking. AI is increasingly performing many of the cognitive activities that once enabled workers to move up the value chain.

MIT’s Daron Acemoglu arrived at a similar conclusion from a different direction. He argues that the key issue is how firms choose to deploy AI. If businesses use AI primarily to replace workers rather than to augment their productivity, the historical pattern of technological progress creating more employment than it destroys might no longer hold. The structure of the emerging AI economy already reflects this logic. Many of today’s most valuable AI companies generate extraordinary market value with remarkably small workforces.

Agentic AI further accelerates this process. Agents no longer automate isolated tasks; they increasingly perform entire workflows: analyzing information, correcting errors, adapting strategies and coordinating complex processes with minimal human intervention.

“For the first time since the Industrial Revolution, labor could cease to be the economy’s scarcest factor of production.”

For companies, the decisive issue is simple: Can AI perform economically valuable tasks at substantially lower cost than humans? Increasingly, for many roles, the answer is yes.

The substitution of labor by machines is unfolding in two waves.

The first affects white-collar work. A junior financial analyst, lawyer, management consultant or software engineer in London or New York may cost an employer 80-100 per hour. Modern language models can already perform many of their tasks for a fraction of a cent. Systems possess another structural advantage. While the knowledge accumulated by an employee spreads only gradually through an organization and often disappears when that employee leaves, improvements made by software are retained and deployed instantly and at scale across an entire system.

The second wave is now reaching the physical economy and the blue-collar population. Humanoid robots developed by companies such as Tesla and China’s Unitree are learning increasingly complex movements through observation and simulation. Their manufacturers hope eventually to reduce operating costs to below $2 per hour. This is in stark contrast to 30-50 per hour for an average American worker.

Research by the International Monetary Fund suggests that nearly 60% of jobs in advanced economies will be affected by artificial intelligence, with almost half facing substantial disruption or substitution. Against that background, a reduction of roughly 30% in total employment over the coming decades no longer appears implausible. Whether the final figure is 20% or 40% is ultimately of secondary importance.

What matters is that, for the first time since the Industrial Revolution, labor could cease to be the economy’s scarcest factor of production. If that is true, the consequences extend far beyond the labor market. They force us to reconsider one of the deepest assumptions of the industrial age.

Shrinking Rich

It is precisely at this point that a possibility emerges that remains almost unthinkable in the discourse today: Population decline, discussed almost exclusively as an economic catastrophe, may prove to be an essential corrective during the intelligence revolution. I call this the 30/30 equilibrium.

The idea is simple. Imagine an advanced economy whose population gradually declines by around 30% over several decades while artificial intelligence and robotics reduce labor demand by a similar magnitude. These developments will not occur simultaneously or at the same pace, yet over time they could broadly offset one another. Fewer people require fewer jobs. As a result, the historical ratio between productive labor and the total population could remain remarkably stable without placing an additional burden on public finances.

The 30/30 equilibrium is, first and foremost, a theory of macroeconomic stabilization in which demographic decline ceases to be an economic disaster and becomes part of the adjustment mechanism. However, it does not create prosperity.

Whether a shrinking society also becomes richer depends on a second variable: capital deepening. As the Solow-Swan growth model demonstrates, long-run prosperity depends less on the size of the labor force than on the amount and productivity of capital available to each worker. If AI and robotics increase productive capital faster than the labor force contracts, output per person continues to rise even while the total workforce declines. Read Noema in print.

If we want an economy’s GDP to stabilize, we need a booster. A 30% decline in the labor force would have to be offset by roughly a 45% increase in capital productivity. This would raise GDP per capita by more than 40%. Given the learning curves already observed in semiconductors, computing power, artificial intelligence and robotics, together with the widening cost advantage of machine intelligence over human labor, such productivity gains no longer appear particularly ambitious.

Now, suppose instead that the population remained constant while productive capital increased by the same 45%. Total output would then expand by roughly 20%. Conventional economics would celebrate this as the superior outcome.

William Stanley Jevons observed in the 19th century that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain’s coal consumption. They increased it. As energy became cheaper, new applications emerged, further expanding demand.

Efficiency produced abundance, but abundance also produced greater resource use. The same dynamic may now apply to intelligence. As AI becomes cheaper, we will almost certainly consume far more of it. This applies to cognitive work as well as to robotics. Silicon Valley celebrates this future as “abundance.” Yet abundance is not necessarily environmentally sustainable. Every additional product made and consumed at a fraction of today’s cost and price still consumes energy and leaves a negative ecological footprint. In addition, AI systems require substantial electricity, computing infrastructure, rare materials and manufactured hardware. Abundance comes at a high cost to the physical world.

“For the first time in history, we may be able to become fewer without becoming poorer. We may even become richer while placing a lighter burden on the natural world.”

From an environmental perspective, allowing the population to decline naturally while increasing prosperity per person may therefore represent a superior equilibrium. For the first time since the Industrial Revolution, the intelligence economy offers us the possibility of choosing such an equilibrium.

This requires abandoning two assumptions inherited from the industrial age.

The first is financial. Modern economies are organized around debt, money creation and asset valuations that all depend on continual expansion. Tomorrow’s economy must become larger than today’s because yesterday’s obligations must be repaid. A “shrinking-rich economy” may ultimately require a monetary and financial system that derives its stability less from ever-expanding debt than from the growing productivity of capital.

The second is geopolitical. “Big is beautiful” belonged to an era in which economic and military strength depended directly on scale. Larger populations meant more workers, more consumers, more inventors, larger armies, bigger markets and greater geopolitical influence. The intelligence economy changes that logic. Human intelligence is scarce, but artificial intelligence expands usable intelligence at an extraordinary pace and cost, making it an abundant resource. Furthermore, technologies such as autonomous drones increasingly erode the traditional military advantages of scale. The same is true for economic influence.

Ecology offers a useful framework. The ecologist Eugene Odum distinguished between pioneer and climax ecosystems. Young forests grow aggressively, consume resources and prioritize speed over sustainability. Mature forests grow little yet contain far greater biomass, complexity, stability and resilience than the pioneer systems from which they emerged.

Human civilization may not be fundamentally different. The fossil-fuel economy was humanity’s pioneer phase. Its success rested on expansion: more people, more energy, more production and more consumption. Artificial intelligence, combined with demographic decline, might allow advanced societies to enter a different stage of development. Technologies such as robotic recycling, AI-managed precision fermentation and closed material loops already point toward an economy capable of creating greater prosperity with fewer material inputs.

The resulting climax society would not be a society of sacrifice. It would be a society that has learned to distinguish growth from prosperity. For the first time in history, we may be able to become fewer without becoming poorer. We may even become richer while placing a lighter burden on the natural world.

The ambition of the 21st century should no longer be to maximize growth but to maximize prosperity: to shrink rich.

Who Inherits The Loom?

If the intelligence economy delivers the productivity gains its advocates expect, it will generate unprecedented wealth. This raises the central political question of the post-labor age: Who receives the surplus?

Under the existing economic order, the answer is clear. The gains will accrue primarily to the owners of capital, not to labor, as ownership determines who has a claim on output. If AI and robotics replace labor as the decisive productive force, then income will shift away from wages and toward those who own the machines, models, data centers, energy systems and platforms through which the new economy operates.

This creates a problem even for the capital owners. Henry Ford understood that workers were producers and consumers. They had to earn wages sufficient to buy the cars they manufactured. The same logic applies to the intelligence economy but in a more unstable form. If machines produce goods while human beings lose the wages with which to buy them, the demand side of the economy weakens. Even the most productive AI economy ultimately depends on customers who can afford to buy what it produces.

Silicon Valley’s preferred answer to this problem is universal basic income (UBI). The idea is simple. The state provides citizens with a minimum income funded through higher taxes, increased public debt or levies on automated production. In the short term, some form of income floor may well be necessary. It could stabilize demand as the population shrinks and cushion the social shock of technological displacement.

But as a permanent settlement, UBI risks becoming a pharmakon: remedy and poison at the same time.

If financed through public debt, UBI injects additional money and purchasing power into the economy without increasing the supply of productive assets, creating inflationary pressure that erodes part of AI’s productivity gains. If financed by taxing production, businesses will ultimately recover much of the additional cost through higher prices, with a similar effect. In both cases, a significant share of the productivity dividend is dissipated rather than translated into higher real living standards.

Economic history offers a warning. In 1795, English magistrates introduced the Speenhamland system, a wage supplement designed to protect rural workers from poverty. It was intended as relief. In practice, it subsidized employers who could continue paying low wages while the public purse made up the difference. It also entrenched the poor’s dependence on local authorities.

The analogy is not exact, but the lesson matters. Income support may ease the transition, but it is unlikely to provide a durable foundation for a post-labor economy.

“What kind of human beings do we wish to become?”

The challenge, therefore, is to distribute the productivity gains of the intelligence economy without eroding them. That requires a financing mechanism that is neither debt-financed nor production-tax-financed.

Here, Karl Marx becomes newly relevant, though perhaps not for the reasons usually assumed. In the “Grundrisse,” he imagined a future in which wealth would no longer depend primarily on immediate labor time, but on the technological appropriation of what he called the “general intellect”: the accumulated knowledge, science and cooperative intelligence of society. Marx’s most contemporary insight was his recognition that knowledge would become the decisive productive force.

Artificial intelligence gives this idea a literal technological form. AI models are not created in a vacuum. They are trained on the accumulated intellectual inheritance of humanity: books, scientific papers, Wikipedia entries, forum discussions, software libraries, images, public archives, open-source code and countless traces of human communication. They also depend on publicly funded research, energy infrastructure, universities, telecommunications networks, roads, water systems and legal protections. The intelligence economy is built by both private firms and a civilizational commons.

Therefore, should the returns from these systems accrue exclusively to private owners, or should society retain a claim on the productive infrastructure that emerged from its collective knowledge?

The 20th century solved the demand problem through wages. Silicon Valley proposes to solve it through transfers. The intelligence economy may ultimately solve it through ownership.

Society’s claim to a universal capital dividend, instead of a UBI, could take the form of ownership, where governments would secure equity stakes, public stakes or sovereign wealth claims in AI infrastructure that depends on public resources, public data and public markets to operate. The proceeds would not flow into general budgets but would instead be distributed directly to citizens as a universal dividend.

Ownership operates differently economically and is not inflationary. It distributes the productivity gains directly at their source, preserving the full efficiency gains of automation while broadening participation in the wealth it creates.

The former wage-earning seamstress would become a shareholder in the loom rather than a dependent of the state. Aristotle imagined a world in which the self-weaving loom abolished the necessity of labor. The intelligence economy gives us the opportunity to decide who inherits it.

The Devil In Paradise

Suppose we succeed. Imagine that artificial intelligence performs most productive labor, demographic decline cushions the adjustment, a new ownership model distributes the gains of automation without sacrificing productivity and advanced societies once again live within ecological limits. Humanity would come remarkably close to Aristotle’s vision of the self-weaving loom. We might finally become Homo curans.

Even then, two deeper challenges remain. The first concerns meaning. More than 70 years ago, Arendt warned of the danger of what she called “worldlessness.” A society organized around work does not automatically become a society of free citizens once work disappears. On the contrary, people might lose the shared public realm in which they experience responsibility, judgment and a sense of purpose. The deeper crisis of the post-labor age may therefore not be unemployment, but meaninglessness.

The anthropologist David Graeber reached a similar conclusion from a different direction. His analysis of “bullshit jobs” suggested that much contemporary employment does not survive because it is socially indispensable, but because modern societies have forgotten how to organize meaning outside paid work.

If artificial intelligence assumes an increasing share of productive labor, society will have to find answers to how to cultivate lives that remain meaningful outside employment.

The second challenge is even more far-reaching. As the world becomes more complex, we increasingly delegate decisions to artificial intelligence. At first, AI merely assists human judgment. Soon it recommends. Eventually, it decides. Every delegation begins as a convenience and may end in dependency. Human judgment gradually atrophies through disuse.

This process is already visible. We delegate navigation to algorithms, communication to recommendation systems, information retrieval to search engines, financial decisions to automated models, partner selection to matching applications and increasingly even legal and administrative decisions to AI-assisted systems. Each individual delegation appears rational. Together, they transform the relationship between human beings and judgment itself.

The logic of intelligent machines is not identical to the logic of human beings. Their purpose is optimization. Ours is judgment. Confusing the two may ultimately prove to be the deepest alignment problem of all.

As these systems increasingly surpass us in specialized domains, the risk is less that they become human than that humans gradually surrender their own capacity for judgment. We may discover too late that we have become second-class decision-makers in a world optimized by machines: Homo algorithmus.

More than 2,000 years ago, Aristotle asked what would happen if the shuttle could weave by itself. Today, that is a reality. But the self-weaving loom leaves us asking: What kind of human beings do we wish to become? Whether the intelligence economy gives rise to Homo curans or Homo algorithmus will not be decided by technology, but by us.

stories.title: Is the Far-Right Wave Receding?
stories.summary: But there is a deeper dissatisfaction with democracy that the far right continues to exploit. The post Is the Far-Right Wave Receding? appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .

stories.body:
Former President of Serbia Aleksandar Vucic and U.S. President Donald Trump (Anna Moneymaker-Pool/Getty Images)

Originally published in Hankyoreh .

The victory of incumbent Lula in the Brazilian presidential election was a surprise. The longtime leftist politician ran second in the first round behind far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro—the son of disgraced former leader Jair Bolsonaro—and no one in the history of Brazilian democracy had come from behind to win in the second round. But by mounting a huge get-out-the-vote effort, Lula defied all predictions.

Lula also defied the current trend in Latin American elections. In the last 18 months, right-wing candidates had won in seven countries, including Chile, Colombia, and Peru. The trend worldwide has been similar, with the far right winning in local elections in Germany, the extremist party of Marine Le Pen leading the polls in France, and the far right participating in governments in Italy, Finland, and the Czech Republic. Far right leaders remain in place in Russia, India, the Philippines, and, for now, Israel.

Is Lula the outlier? Or does he perhaps represent a political course correction?

For those eager to see a political wave in the making, Lula is not the only example of the electoral repudiation of the far right. On the same day as the Brazilian elections, students managed to oust the longtime autocrat Aleksandar Vucic in the equally surprising Serbian elections. Earlier this year, Viktor Orban also lost at the hands of a unified opposition. The massive “blue wave” rejection of Donald Trump in the midterm elections in the United States has continued the trend.

There is a natural feeling among voters in democratic societies to “throw the bums out.” In Latin America, a “pink” wave of progressive politicians like Ecuador’s Rafael Correa and Colombia’s Gustavo Petro has given way to a “brown” wave of ultra-conservative politicians. Voters, especially in today’s quicksilver environment of social media, respond positively to candidates who promise sweeping change. And thus, the political pendulum swings from left to right and back again.

But the far right is not just another conventional option on the political menu. It offers something radically different because it threatens to undermine the very democratic norms by which it has achieved power. In countries like Russia, Hungary, Turkey, and India, right-wing authoritarians have used democratic means—elections, constitutional changes, legal challenges—to weaken democracy. Other leaders have attempted to do away with democracy much more rapidly, as Jair Bolsonaro tried to do when he plotted to overturn the Brazilian elections that Lula won four years ago. Inspired by these rule-breakers, even traditional conservative politicians, like Yoon Suk Yeol in Korea, have attempted to suspend democracy.

And then there’s the case of Donald Trump. The U.S. president was reelected despite his efforts to overturn the 2020 elections that he lost. During his second term, he has attempted to unilaterally change the constitution. He has ignored court orders, bypassed Congress, and waged war against the mainstream media. He has repeatedly called into question the legitimacy of elections.

But Trump now has the lowest approval rating— 31 percent —of his presidency. In the midterm elections, voters rejected Trump’s party. The Democratic Party has easily retaken control of the House of Representatives, and it now has a comfortable margin of control in the Senate as well.

Unlike in Brazil, American voters are prioritizing their pocketbooks. A narrow majority of Brazilians supported Lula despite the country’s problems with debt and inflation. American voters, on the other hand, are abandoning Trump because of the economy—rising gas prices, the impact of sanctions, the consequences of the Iran War. As they demonstrated by electing Trump to a second term, many American voters don’t seem concerned about his anti-democratic rhetoric or actions.

This, more than the specific victories of the far right, is the more distressing takeaway. After all, democracy is not exactly enjoying its finest hour at the moment. Global freedom, according to the latest Freedom House report, declined for the twentieth consecutive year last year, with the United States, Bulgaria, Italy, El Salvador, and Madagascar registering significant deterioration in political and civil liberties.

Voters are turning toward anti-democratic candidates in part because they are disenchanted with democracy itself. Democratic mechanisms just don’t seem up to the task of addressing the threats currently facing the globe. Democracies have proved incapable of slowing climate change or responsibly controlling technologies like AI. Democracies have utterly failed at ensuring broad prosperity in a globalizing economy. If democrats were more successful at dealing with these problems, the far right’s promises of top-down solutions and returning to mythic pasts would not be so appealing.

This deeper problem with democracy suggests that even if the far right loses elections—in Brazil last month, the United States this week, France next year—it will not gracefully surrender the stage. Figures like Yoon Suk Yeol and Jair Bolsonaro can be jailed for their transgressions—and perhaps Trump too will follow in their footsteps. But voters will keep turning to more authoritarian alternatives if democratic institutions don’t deliver and democratic values don’t appeal.

The far right does not offer any better answers to the world’s problems. Its general response to global threats has been to turn its back. The far right supports high tariff walls, more fossil fuel extraction, and stricter controls on immigration. It repudiates all forms of globalization, lumping together neoliberal trade policies with Green energy programs and sensible approaches to immigration. The far right despises democracy not just because it puts controls on autocratic leaders but because of its association with globalization.

This, then, is the essential task of both the left and the center—to devise a new, robust internationalism that provides concrete gains to the average person while also safeguarding the planet for the next generations.

Until this happens, far-right candidates will continue to win. They might lose this or that election. But they will continue to win support with their anti-global agenda, while remaining focused on their ultimate goal of destroying democracy. They don’t want to be subject to the pendulum swings of democratic politics. They want to rip out the pendulum so that they can remain in power indefinitely.

stories.body:
Flavio Bolsonaro (Shutterstock)

In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s electoral victory over Flávio Bolsonaro on October 25 is a monumental win for the left. It could also be the start of perhaps the weakest chapter of his political career after he starts his fourth term on January 5, 2027. After all, he faces a Federal Senate (Upper House) and Chamber of Deputies (Lower House) where the Liberal Party (LP) of Bolsonaro holds the most seats.

After coming in second to Bolsonaro during the general election on October 4, Lula promised that he would get the votes from potential voters who had abstained in the first round. The interim 20 days were filled with often over-the-top appeals by both sides to their constituents.

During the televised debates, Bolsonaro used insults and baiting in his attempts to galvanize voters, appealing to their frustrations regarding corruption, crime, and Lula’s third term. In contrast and enforced by a strong social media presence, Lula used the promise of monetary payments (Pé-de-Meia Universitário) to assist college students with tuition and other expenses. He also pledged to reduce work weeks. Both of his actions might actually hurt the country economically, and they give credence to those who believe that Lula buys his votes. Lula was also bolstered by an increased street team presence (Lula’s Army), a social media footprint that was earlier hampered by Meta, and persistent anti-Trump sentiment generated by U.S. interference in South American politics.

Political scientist Gabriel Elias commented on the increase in Lula’s presence after the first-round election: “I’m feeling more optimistic today, with the massive (Worker’s Party [PT]) demonstrations we’ve seen recently. They may not have the electoral impact many are hoping for, but they leave us much better prepared to face the challenges that will come with the awful makeup of the incoming Congress.”

Reaching the People

Lula is “politically unique,” according to Daniel De Mendonça, professor of political theory at the Federal University of Pelotas. In De Mendonça’s view, Bolsonaro lost because of three main factors. The first is that the initial election focused more on Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes than on the candidates. The second is the long overdue political debates between Lula and Bolsonaro, which turned voters off because of Bolsonaro’s confrontational strategy and arrogant attitude. The third is, De Mendonça continued, Flávio ’s comments regarding the Ana Clara Soares de Oliveira case (2021) in which a military officer shot a five-year-old girl twice, killing her. Bolsonaro represented the officer in court, and this was used by Lula’s Army and spread on social media.

In the period between the two rounds, Bolsonaro had an opportunity to detail a plan for the country. Like his father, however, he offered nothing other than talk under the guise of change.

Cesar Barroso a resident of Rio de Janeiro, who voted for Bolsonaro, remarked after the election results were announced that “the lack of support from the ones [who voted] in the first round” is what lead to the upset loss. Barroso lamented that “it is very difficult to overcome a system that has been entrenched in all the country’s institutions for decades, especially in the judiciary.”

Paulo who resides in Macapá had a much more positive perspective. The election “has brought a sense of comfort to the hearts of Brazilians, who have been through so much. People from across the political spectrum—both left and right—have played a role in this journey.” He added that even members of the right support Lula in escaping from “the phenomenon of Bolsonarism.”

Steering the Ship Around?

Barring bad health, Lula will be 85 when he completes his final term. This leaves the PT with two main issues. They must find a successor and move that individual out of Lula’s shadow. Both issues may be difficult to resolve due to the corruption scandals that enveloped past candidates (e.g., Dilma Rousseff) and the sheer bombastic quality of Lula’s presence and ability to negotiate with all sides regardless of political leanings.

Political scientist Thomás Zicman de Barros described Lula as a “force of charisma,” a modern version of former President Getúlio Vargas (1930–1945, 1951–1954) who was dubbed the “Father of the Poor.” De Barros highlights that the people who truly run the country—and who refer to it as “the big center”—are all conservative local politicians and not open ideologically. This may be where Lula makes the majority of his efforts, which could lead to a lackluster fourth outing as president.

As for the Bolsonaro family, this could be the end of their political careers. The current election was always a make-or-break event for them. This latest loss might push them out of the limelight permanently.

“On Sunday night, I watched in horror as electoral fraud unfolded before my eyes,” Flávio Bolsonaro wrote after the election. “The illegitimate and illegal actions of Lula’s former lawyer allowed a mathematical impossibility to materialize, resulting in Lula gaining over 10 million votes from the first to second round.”

Instead of pushing this version of the election in the courts, Bolsonaro has fled Brazil to the relative safety of his brother Eduardo in South Florida—despite Justice Alexandre de Moraes request for his passport prior to his exodus. Bolsonaro complained that this action was part of making him “a hostage” and an “object of blackmail to protect the corrupt Supreme Court justices from impeachment.” Whether this will lead to a campaign to contest the election is currently unclear. There has been a large drop-off in content on Bolsonaro-related media.

One prominent Bolsonaro remains in the country. Michelle de Paula Bolsonaro, wife of Jair Bolsonaro, won her first Senate seat in Brasilia D.F. during the first round. She may be the one to watch out for, especially if she starts eyeing the presidential position.

Brazilians still deeply distrust the government. That and the greater precarity of the workforce are the two biggest challenges facing Brazil. As De Barros points out, the normal political climate is not just “about politicians getting rich. It’s also economic elites working with the state and with politicians to get rich.” An authoritarian leader could appeal to future voters on an anti-corruption platform.

The Future of Brazil

Shortly after the election results were released, Trump both stated that he “did not want to take sides” but felt that it looked like a “rigged” election. Bolsonaro thanked him and the American people, stating that “President Trump is a great defender of freedom and expression.”

Beyond insults, jabs regarding organized crime, and tariffs, Trump will largely back off. With most of South America already under his influence and no other opportunities being available during the remainder of his term, Brazil is relatively safe from foreign interference.

Brazilians are generally hostile to Trump’s efforts to intervene in Brazilian politics. But they also recognize the advantages of a good relationship with Washington. “We are living through a different kind of war—a war of agreements,” a person from Sáo Pablo told me. “Brazil is expanding through bilateral deals; we have agreements with a large part of the world. We’re the friend to everyone.”

Could he could see Brazil working with the United States under Lula? “Access to American infrastructure would certainly help with capital, but what about the social aspect?” he responded.
