stories.title: Putin not invited to G20 summit in Manchester, says Burnham
stories.summary: The prime minister has said sanctions against Russia mean Putin will not attend the summit in November 2027.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Putin, seen here during a speech in Moscow on Wednesday, has been missing from G20 summits since the Ukraine war

Published 5 November 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Vladimir Putin is not invited to the G20 summit in Manchester.

Asked whether the Russian president would be invited to the annual meeting, which the UK is hosting in November 2027, Burnham said "no" because of sanctions against the Kremlin.

The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

But US president Donald Trump has sparked controversy by inviting Putin to this year's G20, which he will host in Miami in December. The Kremlin has not yet said whether Putin will attend.

Russia is a member of the G20 - a group of 19 nations, the European Union and African Union - while Ukraine is not, but the ongoing war in Ukraine has loomed large over recent summits.

Putin has not attended any major global summit since he launched his invasion and ongoing war in Ukraine.

Asked about inviting him to the G20 in Manchester in 2027, Burnham told The Economist he "will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction" on senior Russian figures.

He said the meeting would provide "a real opportunity" to work with Chinese president Xi Jinping on safety regulations for artificial intelligence (AI).

Pressed on whether the UK could bring the US and China around the same table to agree on global AI supervision, Burnham said: "As I sit here today, that feels challenging, but we've got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI.

"If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.

"So you've got to go into it with that aim."

His decision not to include Putin in next year's gathering in Manchester comes after European diplomats refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in October.

The so-called "family photo" would usually include representatives from all nations in attendance, but this year it was cancelled.

The US decision to invite Lavrov in the first place - which itself came after further public rows between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - also attracted criticism.

Discussing Ukraine, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told Lavrov at the summit: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is."

The UK last hosted the G20 summit in 2009. Next year's two-day event will take place in the Manchester Central Convention Centre in Manchester city centre and host thousands of diplomats and delegates, as well as world leaders.

The government has said it will use its G20 presidency in 2027 to "reinforce global economic stability" and "benefit people in every part of the UK".

stories.title: Could this be the last Bonfire Night for noisy fireworks?
stories.summary: About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, but some campaigners want quieter displays.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 November 2026

Bangers, rockets and screamers have long been part of Bonfire Night - but the traditional celebrations might sound a little different next year.

The government is currently considering reducing the noise limit for fireworks by 50% for those bought in shops for private use, after pressure from campaigners concerned about the impact on nervous animals and people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).

Professionally organised displays would continue to have no maximum limit provided the noise level is not harmful to human health.

About 20 million people enjoy fireworks at home every year, according to industry figures.

Andy Hubble, of the British Fireworks Association (BFA), said displays had already been getting quieter and a balance must be struck to prevent a black market in noisy fireworks springing up.

The end of October sees the start of several celebrations traditionally marked by fireworks and bonfires, including Halloween on 31 October, Guy Fawkes Night on 5 November, and Diwali, which is on 8 November this year.

The government has said an outright ban on the public buying fireworks would not be proportionate.

But Business Minister Kate Dearden said her department was considering "reforms to fireworks legislation, focused on their key harms associated with their misuse - their noise, and contribution to antisocial behaviour – whilst still allowing individuals to enjoy fireworks safely and responsibly for the important community and cultural celebrations they play a part of."

It is already illegal to sell fireworks to under 18s, or to set fireworks off after 23:00, with exemptions for special occasions including Bonfire Night, Diwali, New Year's Eve and Chinese New Year.

But campaigners have raised concerns about the impact of loud bangs on nervous pets.

Dog owner Katherine Alderson, from Clacton-on-Sea, told BBC Breakfast: "It's a nightmare every single year.

"This year I've actually barricaded my bedroom window with numerous layers of insulation to try and keep out the noise of fireworks."

Asked whether reducing the bangs would take the fun out of fireworks, she said she believed displays "should be about the lights and colours" and suggested "a complete ban" on the sale of fireworks to the general public could be the solution.

A woman enjoys fireworks in a crowd of people

But other campaigners say a ban is not needed, including Alan Friggieri, from the charity Combat Stress, which supports veterans with PTSD.

Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons' Business Committee, Friggieri said calls to their helpline jump at this time of year because loud bangs can trigger PTSD symptoms.

"Nothing quite sounds like an AK47 other than fireworks going off - it's that crackle," one veteran who had been shot multiple times had told him.

Friggieri said veterans need to be able to plan around key dates, but he said he was not calling for a ban, because his organisation understands the cultural importance of firework displays.

Calling for better enforcement of existing rules by police to stop antisocial behaviour, BFA vice chairman Hubble warned a ban in Ireland had seen a flourishing black market in firework sales.

"There is a real risk here that if we make fireworks quieter that there is still a demand then we could create an illegal market where fireworks are coming in through internet sales and white van sales," he told BBC Breakfast.

"At the moment we have a really well-regulated market where we have enforcers that know the products and can test them but as soon as these products go undercover then we lose that.

"We could actually create a louder and noisier environment because those are the sorts of fireworks that we're seeing coming in through illegal sales on the internet."

Asked whether it was true that displays were getting noisier, Hubble said: "No, no, it's a lot quieter than it used to be - we used to have bangers and air bombs and and screamer rockets that used to be on sale and they were withdrawn from sale."

The government is considering reducing the maximum noise limit from the current 120dB, equivalent toa thunderclap, to 110dB, which is equivalent to a car horn.

Hubble said a BFA assessment of firework sales shows a 50% noise reduction to 110 dB would impact up to 60% of firework sales to the general public.

Lowering levels to 90DB, equivalent to a lawnmower, as some campaigners want, would affect about 95% of fireworks.

"That's effectively a ban on consumer fireworks, not a modest reduction in noise," he said.

RSPCA advice for people with nervous pets:

Stay calm and show your pet that all is well

Put on music or the TV to help mask firework sounds

Close any windows and do what you can to block out both the noise and the flashes

Keep your environment secure: make sure your pet can't escape if there's a sudden noise

For dogs: let them pace around, if they're whining, barking or hiding, let them

Play with a toy if your pet wants to join in, but don't force them to play

Combat Stress advice for people with PTSD:

Use noise cancelling headphones to reduce the sound of explosions and blackout blinds to block out flashes of light

Use scented candles, diffusers or plug ins to make your home smell good and nothing like those you remember from deployments

Remind yourself you are safe, and focus on the present using breathing and grounding techniques, or with exercise

Ask friends and family to be with you on key dates like Bonfire Night

stories.body:
John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff

W ith four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic.

The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points.

They had been punished as part of a “special campaign to crack down on match-fixing, gambling and corruption in the football industry”, said a joint statement from the Chinese Football Association, the Ministry of Public Security and the General Administration of Sport at the time.

Chengdu were one of the seven to start on zero, above the defending champions Shanghai Port, who lost five points, and the runners-up Shanghai Shenhua who were hit with 10. It robbed the usual favourites of energy and it was all a bit surreal.

It almost felt over as soon as it started with Chengdu opening up a big lead, dropping just two points from the first 12 games while the usual powers struggled to get going.

Chengdu is a major city known more for its fiery Sichuan cuisine, genteel temples and cute pandas than football, despite English attempts to change that. In 2006, Sheffield United bought a local club but the Chengdu Blades were eventually dissolved in 2015. Four years later, City Football Group bought a stake in Sichuan Jiuniu but then moved the club to the southern city of Shenzhen in 2024.

Chengdu Rongcheng were formed in 2018, coming up through the divisions to finally, this season, be within touching distance of the championship. But just two wins from the past 13 and three defeats in a row mean the leaders are not limping to the line but have collapsed right next to it.

It should have been over weeks ago. On 10 October, more than 40,000 fans were ready to celebrate the title but an added‑time goal from Alberto Quiles gave Tianjin Jinmen Tiger a 1-0 win and postponed the celebrations. Next up was a trip to Shanghai Port but that ended in a 3-0 defeat. The penultimate game of the season came against challengers Dalian Yingbo, when again, just avoiding defeat was needed. It was another painful experience as they lost 1-0 after missing a first-half penalty and having a 90th-minute equaliser ruled out by the video assistant referee.

Chengdu have not scored in almost seven hours of football while Dalian are the form team with four consecutive wins. If they win a fifth against Tianjin then Chengdu need a point at fourth‑placed Shandong Taishan as the league is decided by head-to-head results before goal difference. Not many think they will. Even fewer hope so. Dalian and the 60,000 fans who attend home games are the people’s choice. Chengdu are not popular because their fans have developed a poor reputation. Last November, the club were fined about $70,000 (£52,200) after some home supporters racially abused Henan FC’s Ghanaian striker Frank Acheampong, just weeks after a punishment of $3,000 after travelling supporters at a Champions League game in South Korea threw bottles at the Ulsan HD players.

Whatever happens it is an unexpected and dramatic ending to a season that started in shock and the usual negative international headlines that surround Chinese football. The grandstand finish is welcome and average attendances have risen. They are poised to finish at about 30,000, a considerable jump from 25,755 last season and, by some distance, the best in Asia. Regional leagues have been enjoying some popularity too, showing that there is genuine love for the game in the country; a passion that grows better when it is organic from the bottom rather than organised from the top.

after newsletter promotion

The national side is still a problem, though, and even for a fanbase well accustomed to disappointment the recent 5-0 defeat against Palestine at home, the fourth-biggest loss in history, was tough to take. As one journalist said, being thrashed by Brazil, Japan and Wales is one thing, but Palestine was another. There were some mitigating circumstances in that a number of national team players were at the Asian Games, where China actually performed well, losing narrowly against South Korea in the bronze final.

There are signs that the gap behind Korea is not as wide as it used to be. China reached the final of the under-17 and under-23 Asian championships this year before losing both against Japan. Compared with the rest of Asia’s best, young Chinese players are closing the gap at a technical and tactical level. Exporting more players to Europe is necessary to play at a higher level and if that happens, that senior national shirt may feel a little lighter.

Failure can, however, be hard to shake off as Chengdu Rongcheng may well find out if they mess this up.

stories.title: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
stories.summary: Co-founder of Palestine Action, Huda Ammori, is challenging the government's decision to proscribe the group.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Supporters of Palestine Action were arrested outside the Supreme Court, where a hearing over the group's ban began on Wednesday

Published 4 November 2026

The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience from law-abiding protesters, the Supreme Court has been told.

Opening a major legal challenge to the group's proscription last year, lawyers for co-founder Huda Ammori said that no other protest organisation had been treated the same way.

They told the five justices that the UK's highest court had never before had to consider whether banning a group under terrorism legislation was compatible with freedom of speech and protest.

Twenty-seven protesters were arrested outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday as the hearing took place, the Metropolitan Police said.

Lawyers for Ammori told the court that thousands of elderly people, many veterans of other radical causes, had been arrested for holding up signs supportive of the group since its proscription.

Home Office figures seen by the BBC indicate that there have been more than 4,000 arrests so far at protests in which people have held up signs supportive of the group.

In practice, many demonstrators have been arrested more than once, with 1,200 charges authorised by prosecutors to date. Those trials are in limbo until the outcome of this case.

Henry Blaxland KC told the court that "far from depriving Palestine Action of the oxygen of publicity" and "far from discrediting its brand", proscription of the group has had the opposite effect.

"All it's done is to pour fuel on to a fire of one of the most publicly-contested issues of our time," he said.

"It was disproportionate to do that and in my submission completely unnecessary."

During often tense exchanges with the judges, Ammori's team accepted that Palestine Action could not be described as an ordinary and peaceful protest group.

They said that its members had carried out "direct action" protests by occupying or vandalising firms linked to Israel's military - with only three of 385 incidents assessed by the Home Secretary as constituting an offence under the Terrorism Act.

The UK's definition of terrorism includes incidents of serious damage to property for a cause - and at least two break-ins at defence firms have been described in criminal courts as having caused millions in damage.

Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that the judges had to put aside allegations of criminality - for which the state had many powers - and consider whether the Home Secretary's decision to label the group as terrorists had been disproportionate.

"Palestine Action was proscribed on the basis of less than one per cent of its actions over five years assessed as falling within the outer limits of a definition of terrorism," he said.

"The Home Secretary's own experts confirmed the vast majority of its direct action would not constitute an act of terrorism on the basis that any damage to property is typically more minor. Common tactics include graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation, and lock-ons."

One Palestine Action member has been convicted and jailed of fracturing a police officer's back with a sledgehammer - but the court was told that the group had never advocated such violence.

Opposition from Jewish groups

The Supreme Court has received arguments from free speech campaigners, arguing the ban interferes with the right to protest.

But another submission from a coalition of Jewish groups argued that Palestine Action was a "sinister" organisation intent on attacking its community interests.

"The Court of Appeal [following earlier hearings] rightly concluded that PA is a violent organisation concerned in terrorism with a wide range of targets," said Adam Wagner KC in written submissions for the Jewish communal groups.

He continued: "Its activities are often undertaken covertly with no suggestion of restraint or proportionality, and that at the point it was proscribed it had an escalating trajectory of seriousness and an expanding focus."

Wagner said Palestine Action's "crosshairs" had moved from targeting Elbit, a defence firm with an Israeli parent company, to "figures or institutions deemed by PA to be 'Zionist'".

"Because most British Jews and Jewish institutions have a connection with Israel, a campaign against institutions PA's activists consider to be 'complicit' with Israel is, in practice, a campaign that threatens the mainstream Jewish community," he said.

However, Jewish Bloc, a group that campaigns in solidarity with Palestinians, told has also written to the court to say that claims that PA targeted their community were a "fundamental misrepresentation of the underlying evidence".

Rachel Scott KC, for the organisation, told the justices: "Neither the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) nor the Community Security Trust (CST) have any democratic mandate. Claims that either organisation can be viewed as the voice of British Jews must therefore be viewed with very significant caution.

"The framing of PA as an organisation which threatened and intimidated 'the Jewish Community' is demonstrably false and a deliberate elision. The evidence instead shows that it targeted entities, organisations and institutions with an established link to Israel's illegal activities against the Palestinian people."

The case continues on Thursday with a judgment expected at a later date.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Republicans’ crushing setback will play out in stock markets, inflation, interest rates and economic growth

Donald Trump’s loss of control of the House of Representatives and the Senate has put the world economy on notice for an unpredictable final two years of his presidential term.

After Democrats swept aside his Republican party in the midterm elections, analysts said the prospect of a highly erratic lame-duck president would have significant implications for financial markets, growth, inflation, government borrowing costs and living standards.

Here are the biggest expected consequences for the US economy and for other countries.

Stock markets

Markets initially dropped in early trading in Asia overnight but rallied as investors weighed up the midterm results.

Investors typically dislike uncertainty and political chaos. The fact that the president conceded the result and acknowledged the impact of the Iran war has been taken as a positive in markets. However, his warning that he will become “Mr Veto” raises the prospect of a turbulent finale to his time in the White House.

Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg, said the result showed that US voters had “rejected Trump and his somewhat authoritarian penchant for crony capitalism. [That] shows that US institutions and its checks and balances work. That is a positive, in my view.”

Much of the outlook for stock markets, inflation and growth is contingent on the war in the Middle East and the pace of the advance of artificial intelligence.

Traders expect the Democrats to take a tougher line on AI regulation and the datacentre rollout, raising questions over a driver of stock market growth. There are also concerns that Trump, with the midterms out of the way and his control over domestic policy weakened, could take a more aggressive approach to foreign policy, with the potential to intensify the war in Iran.

Inflation

The cost to US households from surging inflation triggered by a deeply unpopular war, alongside a chaotic tariff policy that has devastated small businesses, was key to the midterm result. US diesel prices surged to a record high in August , while the headline inflation rate has risen to 3.7%.

The US-Israeli invasion of Iran, leading to the closure of the critical strait of Hormuz, reignited global inflationary pressures amid the biggest energy price shock of the modern age.

The oil price fell back on Wednesday, dropping by as much as 9% to trade below $100 a barrel for the first time in a month, as investors digested the midterm results amid hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough on Iran. Trading at about $94, Brent crude, the international benchmark, remains significantly higher than its prewar level of about $70. As a consequence, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects global headline inflation to rise to 4.7% this year, with energy-importing countries hardest hit.

The possibility of Trump ramping up hostilities against Iran would add to the inflationary shock, but it would also further add to his unpopularity.

Interest rates

Higher inflation has forced central banks to raise interest rates, with the US Federal Reserve defying pressure from Trump by increasing the cost of borrowing for the first time since 2023.

Against a volatile backdrop in the war and as inflationary pressures persist, investors anticipate at least one more rate increase from the Fed. The Bank of England is expected on Thursday to raise rates , while the European Central Bank is also expected to push up borrowing costs.

After losing control of Congress, the Republicans will lack the votes to confirm new appointments to critical public bodies, including new Fed governors. Trump could still use his veto powers, which can be overturned only if two-thirds of both chambers agree.

Government finances

Higher inflation and interest rates triggered by the Iran war have driven up borrowing costs, adding to the pressure on countries with high levels of public debt.

In the US, the logjammed political system will face its first major test on 11 December, when politicians have to agree to authorise government spending to avoid a shutdown . The gridlock could prevent Trump from launching new tax and spending measures, which could cut two ways, restricting the capacity for fiscal stimulus to boost the economy, but also limiting a further rise in borrowing and debt.

Analysts say the crushing midterm defeats for Maga candidates will hurt the president’s authority and could pave the way for more cooperation between Republicans and Democrats in Congress.

Economic growth

Analysts say political turbulence and presidential actions on trade and immigration could put US growth at risk, but inflation and, most importantly, the prospects for de-escalation in the Middle East are the main factors to watch.

Investors are wary that a clampdown by the Democrats on AI could hit investment and growth in the US. The spillovers from the tech boom have been felt around the globe, with AI investment helping to bolster the UK economy.

However, tech industry leaders were already cooling on the rollout of AI amid concerns over cyber risks. Many investors also feared the emergence of a bubble in the US stock market. Analysts at Allianz say the scale of AI investment, and its capacity to power global economic growth, could mean the left-right political playbook is less predictable than in the past. Environmental and social impacts are also increasingly important considerations.

As recently as last month the IMF forecast that US growth would remain stable at 2.3% this year and next, despite the heightened risks to activity caused by the Iran war and the uncertain path for AI investment.

Analysts at Berenberg said US growth could slow to about 1.5% in 2028 amid political gridlock, a slowdown over AI and a drag from Trump’s crackdown on immigration. As a result, the US would contribute less to global growth than before, they said.

stories.body:
Purchasing manager’s index at eight-month high, bolstered by spending on AI as firms regain momentum lost to Iran war

The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday after a closely watched survey showed growth across the UK’s services sector leapt last month to an eight-month high, bolstered by spending on artificial intelligence.

S&P Global’s survey of the services sector in October showed businesses regained much of the momentum they lost after the start of the Iran war, but also felt the impact of a renewed spurt of input price inflation, which accelerated to a five-month high.

Officials at the Bank have become concerned about inflation after the consumer prices index (CPI) rose from 3.1% in August to 3.5% in September .

While the nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC), which sets interest rates, has been split in recent months , a majority is expected to vote on Thursday for 0.25 percentage point increase to 4%.

Tim Moore, the economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a survey of the manufacturing sector earlier this week also showed businesses facing strong price pressures.

He said: “These signals underscore the near-certainty of a Bank of England rate hike in November and collectively raise the likelihood of further Bank of England policy tightening into 2027.”

Financial markets expect three further increases in the cost of borrowing, although most City economists believe inflation is likely to peak in the spring of next year, allowing the Bank to limit the number of extra interest rate rises to one or two.

Moore said service providers indicated the fastest upturn in activity since February and “a solid rebound in new orders”.

The S&P Global services purchasing manager’s index (PMI), which gauges growth across sector, rose from 52.1 to 52.8. A reading above 50 indicates a period of expansion.

Bigger workloads prompted businesses in the services industry to take on additional staff in October, the survey found.

This ended two years of continuous job cutting across the sector, with many businesses during that period saying that they were responding to higher labour and business costs, or not replacing employees who left.

Moore said the survey suggested an “increase in economic resilience despite challenges from geopolitical tensions, elevated cost pressures and subdued consumer confidence”.

“Greater workloads were attributed to an improved pipeline of sales opportunities, particularly those linked to AI investment spending,” he added.

The sector has benefited from the demand for AI applications and software services associated with the boom in datacentre construction.

Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the economic forecasters the Item Club, said official data also pointed to a surge in activity in the IT and professional services sectors.

after newsletter promotion

He cautioned that growth in business-to-business services was not being matched on the high street, which has continued to be badly affected by a dip in consumer confidence.

“With at least some of that strength reflecting businesses’ rapid adoption of AI technologies, we expect pockets of strength to sustain momentum into next year. But in a two-speed economy, consumer-facing services will come under increasing pressure as households’ spending power is squeezed,” Swannell said.

He added: “An interest rate hike looks nailed on at tomorrow’s MPC meeting. And today’s data only adds to the weight of evidence.”

Moore said about four in 10 of the services sector survey panel reported an increase in their input prices, while only 1% experienced a decline.

It is unclear how much services firms will pass on higher input costs to consumers, pushing up inflation. Some members of the MPC have said they are prepared to wait for more evidence while others have indicated they will vote to quell even modest increases in prices.

Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said there was a sign that services businesses were absorbing costs, but not by enough to prevent a rate rise.

The services output price balance dropped to 56.9, from 57.8 in September. “We estimate this is consistent with underlying services inflation rising about 4.1%, down from the latest official reading of 4.4% but still too high for the MPC to stand pat,” Wood said.

Meanwhile, inflation in the eurozone rose to a three-year high of 4% last month on surging energy and food costs, up from 3.8% in September. The increase makes a rate rise in December by the European Central Bank more likely after it left borrowing costs unchanged last week.

stories.title: Poundland owner in crunch talks as retailer's collapse looms
stories.summary: Gordon Brothers will meet Jonathan Reynolds on Wednesday as the investment firm faces scrutiny over Poundland.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 November 2026

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has met the US-based owners of Poundland as the government hopes to save the retailer from collapse.

The discount chain is on the brink of insolvency and Gordon Brothers, which bought it for £1 last June, has rejected a takeover bid which could have saved the 12,000 jobs currently at risk.

A meeting was due to be held on Thursday but was brought forward as the scramble to secure a rescue deal for the firm intensifies.

Gordon Brothers said it is "pursuing all avenues through the sales process" but that Poundland has faced several years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable".

The firm said it is "engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties".

It added: "When Gordon Brothers acquired the business, it was in distress and required a radical restructure, urgent operational change and significant funding, which we provided to support the company's ability to trade."

Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of the business has not been made.

On Wednesday, a source close to business secretary said Reynolds "has been firm that Gordon Brothers must do everything in their power to protect jobs and provide certainty for workers".

"He is pleased to have secured this commitment from Gordon Brothers in the meeting and will continue to hold the company to account and closely monitor developments," the source added.

It is understood that Gordon Brothers made a commitment in the meeting to prioritise bids that will protect workers and units.

However, it is still unclear whether the US investment firm will keep the business together or break it up.

Meanwhile, MPs say they have called in Poundland's owners for questioning on Wednesday 11 November to explain their role in the discount retailer's looming insolvency.

Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament's business committee, said: "Every report suggests Poundland is a viable, profitable business with a future ahead of it and without good reason to let it crash and burn - and then to break it up and sell it off piece by piece.

"We are asking Gordon Brothers to appear before Parliament to explain themselves and tell us just what it is that's preventing them from accepting the fully-funded deal on the table to save more than 12,000 jobs."

Business Minister Kate Dearden and union representatives met Poundland's managing director Barry Williams on Wednesday.

Mr Williams told the BBC that Poundland is profitable and sales were growing.

"We're back in profit and it has a bright future ahead of it if it's allowed to deliver that," he said.

Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until next Thursday.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Adam Turner: We would lose "a few million" if Poundland went under

Asked what his message for Poundland's owner was, Burnham said Gordon Brothers should "focus on the people in your employment" and "come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores".

"There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let's find it," he added.

The meeting comes after a major Poundland supplier has said it will lose millions of pounds if the retailer goes bust.

Adam Turner, sales director at Bradford-based Highcrest Retail Brands, said Poundland was one of its biggest customers and its collapse would cost it "a few million" in lost sales.

The family owned business mainly sells confectionery to Poundland and turns over about £50m.

Turner said the firm becoming insolvent would leave a substantial gap in its balance sheet next year.

Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", Turner said. But he warned other medium and small suppliers to the retailer have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they".

This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.

Not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall, he told the BBC on Wednesday.

He said he was "amazed" Poundland was being put into administration, pointing to the profitability of the company.

"Also, there's two offers on the table from some really good people," he added.

"All I'm asking is for Gordon Brothers to see if they can put a deal together."

Gordon Brothers said Walsall-based Poundland is "still not cash generative at a sustainable level" because of the economic issues it faces.

If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises.

However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present – meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.

Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm Published 3 days ago

High stock levels

If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" – although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent.

Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit.

"It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years.

"It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added.

Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell.

One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations – selling off stock from collapsed businesses.

One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" – most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas.

Ministers' questions

Dearden has said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but that ministers want "clarity" on the plans for the retailer.

"It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added.

Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees if Poundland collapses.

The head of Gordon Brothers' European operations reportedly told the government that the firm stood by its stewardship and had given Poundland £85m in additional financing since its purchase in 2025.

stories.title: UK commits to 'time-bound' talks on slavery apology
stories.summary: British diplomats are looking to offer reassurance that there is a sense of urgency to deal with the issue, even if a date for doing so is not yet confirmed, Chris Mason writes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham has ruled out reparations but is open to a formal apology

Published 5 November 2026

The UK has signed up to "structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith" talks that address the "historical harms" of the transatlantic slave trade, Commonwealth leaders in Antigua have said.

The formal conclusions marking the end of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, known as the communique, is the joint text setting out what has been agreed.

The 18 page document , external includes a paragraph in which the leaders "welcome the agreement of the Government of the United Kingdom to engage in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms".

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened the door to a formal apology on behalf of the UK for its role in the slave trade, while ruling out the prospect of reparations.

Officials said the timeframe for the talks would be agreed at a later date, though the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has suggested they are likely to conclude in around a year.

Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders' summit in Manchester next November, Miliband told BBC Newscast , external : "Broadly speaking, yes."

The communique was signed after the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda

The rationale among British diplomats in committing to the wording in the communique is to try to offer reassurance that there is a sense of urgency to deal with the issue, even if a date for doing so is not yet confirmed.

This will be determined, sources said, in the "structured dialogue" the UK is promising with countries that have long demanded that the pain and lasting legacies of the slave trade are, as they see it, properly addressed.

Burnham said his "new approach with the Commonwealth" had been "well received" at the summit.

He said it had "been the most successful meeting of the Commonwealth in recent times," adding that "the King's words have resonated powerfully here and we're really pleased with how it's gone".

King Charles III, speaking in his role as Head of the Commonwealth, told the meeting: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other Members of our Commonwealth.

"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

stories.title: More asbestos found in Parliament, as MPs urged to get on with revamp
stories.summary: MPs told it's crunch time for a decision on refurbishment amid warnings of a Notre Dame-style fire.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Palace of Westminster and wider parliamentary estate has a web of old cables in its basement (right)

Published 5 November 2026

More asbestos has been discovered in Parliament, the BBC has learnt, as MPs come under pressure to sign off on a major revamp of the crumbling home of UK democracy.

Known asbestos items in the Palace of Westminster and wider parliamentary estate, such as insulation, roofing, floor tiles and ropes, now number more than 1,650 - an increase of 500 since 2021.

It comes as the government considers holding a vote on refurbishing Parliament, which could cost up to £40bn and take 61 years, after years of indecision and delay.

The Commons public accounts committee this week warned it was "crunch time" for Parliament's restoration, with every additional year of delay costing taxpayers £420m.

More asbestos items were found during surveys in preparation for the long-awaited refurbishment project, parliamentary authorities said.

Asbestos has been identified as one of the main reasons for the refurbishment, given the dangers to human health when its fibres are airborne. While asbestos is largely fireproof, surrounding fire and heat can release fibres over long distances.

In the past five years, 700 items of asbestos have been removed from Parliament but the total has still risen, a Freedom of Information request by the BBC found.

Under Health and Safety Executive guidelines, most of it is classed as low risk in concealed areas, meaning it is less likely to be disturbed, but almost 200 items are classed as medium risk meaning they may require remedial works.

A spokesperson for UK Parliament said its "absolute priority is the safety of the those who work on and visit the parliamentary estate" with improved asbestos monitoring, new awareness training, and plans to further remove it.

Kris Gledhill, the son of former Labour MP Alice Mahon who died in 2022 of malignant mesothelioma - a type of cancer linked to asbestos exposure - told the BBC "asbestos should never be considered low risk".

Alice Mahon was Labour MP for Halifax from 1987 until 2005

"A precautionary approach should be adopted: this includes assessing the fact that in addition to the risks from buildings deteriorating over time, there are also risks of damage from extreme weather events, floods and fire, and from disturbances caused during renovation and maintenance work," he said.

"Alice was well aware of the risks relating to asbestos and mesothelioma," he added.

"She was able to identify two workplaces where she might well have been exposed, one of which was the Palace of Westminster."

The Commons authorities told the BBC "an asbestos-free building cannot be achieved in practice" because that would require demolition or extensive damage to the fabric of the building.

Dr Hannah Moody, chief executive of charity Mesothelioma UK which campaigns on asbestos-related diseases, said she backs introducing a national asbestos register and the phased removal of asbestos from public buildings.

"Although asbestos was banned in 1999, it remains present in many public buildings across the UK and continues to cause serious illness and work-related deaths, including from the aggressive cancer, mesothelioma," she said.

Workers should be given health and safety advice to manage the risks, she added.

'Notre Dame-like flames'

The findings come as the Commons Public Accounts Committee on Wednesday published the results of its inquiry into Parliament's restoration and renewal (R&R) , external programme, which is exploring options to revamp the site.

Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the Conservative MP who chairs the committee, told the BBC that if a small fire broke out in the building "the whole lot would go up" - with 24-hour fire patrols in place.

"Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building's roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life," he added.

He said this was a "real and rising... grave risk" and criticised "a political allergy to gripping the nettle" of refurbishing Parliament after years of delay.

Sewage pumping equipment in the bowels of Parliament dates back to Victorian times - and some steam vessels sit next to high voltage electricity

The committee said there was enough information for MPs and peers to vote on a way forward before the end of this year.

The BBC understands government whips have discussed holding a debate and vote by then, but no date has been scheduled.

This vote would decide whether to proceed with up to £3bn of initial works and narrow down four current options, ahead of a final decision by 2030.

One proposed option would see MPs and peers move out of the site for up to 24 years from 2032, costing up to £15.6bn.

Another involves moving only the House of Lords out of the building, costing £39bn and taking 61 years.

Among the "critical" setbacks the committee identified were an overcomplex decision-making process and delays in acquiring a temporary home for the Lords in the nearby Queen Elizabeth II conference centre, which is owned by the government.

The scale of Labour’s progressive offer, it was made clear, would be umbilically linked to its ability to generate a significant uptick in GDP.

“Growth in every postcode” is also the early mantra of Andy Burnham’s government. The prime minister swept to power partly by running on Greater Manchester’s record as the UK’s fastest-growing city region while he was mayor. Echoing Mr Starmer’s approach, Mr Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, told the Labour party conference in September: “Without growth, there is no social democracy.”

But as the economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal suggest in the latest edition of the Guardian’s new Radical Thinking podcast, that is a flawed and politically unhelpful linkage to make. In a transformed geopolitical environment, they argue, the notion that former levels of growth can be restored is likely to prove a chimera. Just as importantly – as the contrast between Manchester’s booming city centre and hard-pressed towns such as Oldham and Wigan illustrates – better growth rates would not solve entrenched problems of affordability in places unlikely ever to become hubs for advanced manufacturing or financial services.

Yet neither of those assertions mean that an ambitious egalitarian politics must be ruled out. “We need to say: ‘How do low-income places work?’,” Prof Williams says. “What do we need to do to get them to work better?” Or as Prof Johal puts it: “What are the basics, the necessities that we need … for people to have a decent civilised life?” At the most fundamental level, a more ambitiously redistributive fiscal approach can bring bills down for the less well-off. More broadly, shifting resources into the essential building blocks of every local community – transport, utilities, care networks and other social and physical infrastructure – can improve everyday lives by restoring collective control over public goods.

Mr Burnham’s signature move as mayor – the decision to take Greater Manchester’s buses back under public control and cap fares – suggests a shared agenda here. But the prime minister has sent mixed messages when it comes to “ Manchesterism ” – the place-based economic strategy that he wishes to export to the nation. As the role of the United Arab Emirates in the city’s modern development comes under scrutiny, Mr Burnham’s version of “ business-friendly socialism ” is a political philosophy in need of greater definition. Devolution should involve funnelling local power downwards and outwards, rather than upwards to Abu Dhabi-type investors in the indiscriminate pursuit of growth.

A greater focus on the “ foundational ” economy described by Prof Williams and Prof Johal can help with that project. One of Mr Burnham’s last acts as mayor was to sign off on a mayoral development corporation for the town of Middleton , near Manchester. Its agenda is being shaped by residents and local business owners, with the aspiration that local economic networks can be “rewired” and the provision of everyday essentials be reconfigured and improved. Given proper backing from Westminster, social democrats do not need to wait for growth before they can begin improving lives.

stories.title: Chris Mason: The US elections will change Trump - how will Burnham react?
stories.summary: The big question for the British government is does defeat at home make it more likely that President Trump gets angrier abroad?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 November 2026

The first public words from the prime minister after the American midterm elections were instantly revealing about contemporary international politics and diplomacy.

"Well, President Trump has accepted the results," Andy Burnham said.

It is not an observation British leaders have frequently had to make about recent American presidents - that they are not disputing the result of elections in their own country. But what would previously have been taken for granted no longer can be.

Burnham remains in the foothills of establishing a relationship with the president – so far it has amounted to a handful of phone calls and one face-to-face meeting at the United Nations in New York in September.

As he continues to attempt to build a rapport with Donald Trump, he will be doing so with a president in a wildly different political situation than when Sir Keir Starmer was trying to build bridges with him.

No longer is this a story of an extraordinary comeback, but of a midterm president seemingly punished for the consequences of a foreign war the type of which he had originally promised to avoid.

Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results Published 1 day ago

Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad Published 1 day ago

And it is noticeable that the British government's public reaction is grounded too in the consequences of the war with Iran: the cost of living.

"I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all and that's the cost of living," the prime minister said.

"But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia."

Within government the Iran war and its consequences, particularly on energy prices, is widely seen as the biggest individual contributor among the many factors currently driving up the cost of living.

And, bluntly, it is one that puts many, including many of America's allies, in alignment with many in America, Democrat and Republican, who when asked why these elections went as they did, point at the prices displayed outside any petrol station.

Speaking before the votes in America were counted, the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband reflected on this when I spoke to him on BBC Newscast , external .

When I asked him specifically if he feared that a domestically humiliated Trump may prove more belligerent internationally, it was to the Iran war the foreign secretary referred.

He didn't offer a direct answer to my question, but chose instead to say this: "I know that one of the biggest responsibilities of the whole government, frankly, is the cost of living situation at home, and we know one of the biggest contributors to the cost of living situation is, frankly, the conflict."

"The Strait of Hormuz being not exactly closed, but not properly open, not free-flowing, and that is hitting families at home," he said.

"We know that we need a diplomatic way out of this conflict, and so that is one of the things that we're working on. It's something I talked to the US Secretary of State about at the G20, and it's something we continue to work on," he added.

The foreign secretary met Marco Rubio at the meeting in Atlanta last week.

But the big question for the British government, and so many others, is does defeat at home make it more likely that President Trump gets angrier abroad?

Or, do America's traditional allies, the UK, the European Union, Canada, Australia and others feel more strident and willing to work with Donald Trump's domestic political opponents to try to challenge and restrain a weakened president?

The answers to these two final questions will determine much in world affairs in the next couple of years.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andrew Bailey then hints that the Bank could well raise interest rates again, following today’s hike to 4% , unless the Iran war ends.

He tells reporters in London:

double quotation mark Today’s increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. That is not inevitable. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase.

Closing summary

Time to wrap up.

The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to come to combat rising inflation unleashed by the Iran war.

Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the move, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase.

The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices persistently above $100 in recent months, as hopes have evaporated of a deal that could reopen the key strait of Hormuz .

As a result, the Bank now expects UK inflation to rise to 4.9% in the middle of next year – up from 3.2% in its last economic forecast, in July. Inflation hit 3.5% in September , as measured on the consumer prices index.

The decision, which will hit mortgage borrowers, comes a week after John Healey used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers. Echoing the Office for Budget Responsibility’s gloomy forecasts for living standards , the MPC expects real post-tax income to fall this year and next.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, told reporters in London:

double quotation mark Today’s increase should not be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. That is not inevitable. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase.

Here’s what it means for you:

The tech-heavy US Nasdaq share index is on track for its worst day in 18 months after slumping by up to 5% on Thursday amid growing signs that the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation following this week’s midterm elections .

Amid widespread losses on Wall Street, the Nasdaq composite tumbled into ‘correction territory’ – more than 10% below its recent record high. The index was heading for its biggest one-day fall since April 2025 when Donald Trump announced his ‘liberation day’ tariffs on US trading partners.

Worries over massive AI spending gripped the New York stock market, and rippled out to other bourses worldwide, as investors anticipated tougher scrutiny of data-centre expansion plans.

Chip stocks led the slump, with memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 19% and hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 16.5%.

AJ Bell: Panic has set in

“After initially seeming to shrug off concerns about what a Democrat blue wave in the midterm elections might mean for the AI trade, panic set in on Thursday,” says AJ Bell head of financial analysis Danni Hewson.

double quotation mark “The Nasdaq lost more than $1.8 trillion worth of value in intraday trading to enter correction territory, down at least 10% from the most recent highs attained in early October. Investors are fearful of a regulatory backlash against the AI sector from newly elected Democratic lawmakers.”

VIX fear index has jumped

Wall Street’s ‘fear index’, the VIX, has jumped by 40% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.

AI contagion spreads to London

The slump on Wall Street has rippled across to the London stock market too.

The FTSE 100 share index has closed for the night, down 46 points or 0.4% at 10,782 points.

Earlier this morning the ‘Footsie’ had been up over 100 points.

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, says:

double quotation mark ‘Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard, with a steep sell-off on the Nasdaq, and the S&P 500 sending shockwaves rippling to other markets. Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction. Chip stocks have been the hardest hit with AMD down 13%, Nvidia falling around 7% and Intel another 5.5%. The contagion is spreading - the FTSE 100, which had been on the front foot and is far less exposed to big tech, has now erased its earlier gains and turned negative. Even a tech-lite index with defensive appeal hasn’t been able to shrug off this big case of the jitters.

Wall Street slumping

Back on Wall Street, the Dow Jones industrial average (DJIA) has slumped by 2.5%, or 1,346 points, as shares retreat sharply.

Both the S&P 500 share index and the tech-focused Nasdaq has hit their lowest levels since late July, and on track for their biggest one-day drop in five months.

Chip giant Nvidia is leading the selloff on the DJIA , down 8%, followed by Goldman Sachs which has dropped by 6.5%.

Oxford Economics: Hawkish MPC puts a December hike on the table

A December hike in UK interest rates is now “on the table”, argues consultancy Oxford Economics , following today’s rise.

Oxford Economics believes that December’s Monetary Policy Committee meeting “looks like a coin flip”, with oil and natural gas prices set to be the decisive factor.

Their chief UK economist Andrew Goodwin reckons the committee’s messaging was more hawkish than before.

double quotation mark “Higher energy futures prices and more evidence of domestic resilience both increase the risk of second-round effects emerging. The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike in December or February is likely.”

Nasdaq falls into correction territory

America’s technology share index, the Nasdaq Composite, has fallen into correction territory.

The Nasdaq Composite is down 4% today, as tech stocks drop sharply, and is now more than 10% below its record closing high.

Tesla and SpaceX shares slide as midterms pain continues

Oil and gas aren’t the only volatile elements in the markets today, following the events of the last 48 hours.

Over on Wall Street, Elon Musk’s businesses are being hit in the aftermath of the midterm election results.

Shares in Tesla and SpaceX are both down around 9% in early trading, adding to losses yesterday that wiped billions of dollars off both company’s valuation.

The midterms have been something of a disaster for Musk.

He contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress – and then watched the Democrats rack up a series of election wins.

Voters across the US also voted for bans or restrictions on datacentre development, in a backlash against AI.

Bank rate hike: What the economists say

Several economists are arguing that today’s rise in UK interest rates is not the start of a long cycle of rate hikes.

Sanjay Raja , Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, says today’s move is an “insurance policy” against the danger ofsecond-round effects (a wage-price spiral), arguing:

double quotation mark Today’s hike merely adds a dose of policy restriction to an already restrictive policy stance. Moreover, with financial conditions having tightened materially since March, the case to go much further isn’t as strong as it may have been in the Bank’s previous hiking cycle back in 2022. With signs of second-round effects remaining minimal at this juncture, we retain our view for one more hike with Bank Rate peaking at 4.25%. And perhaps the bigger question from today’s decision is whether the next hike comes in December or February. There is a clear risk that the MPC could go earlier – this will be something to watch in the coming weeks and will likely be determined by forthcoming inflation outturns as well as developments in the Middle East (with the last 48 hours delivering some good news on energy price expectations).

Modupe Adegbembo, economist at investment bank Jefferies , believes another hike is likely, but not a foregone conclusion, telling clients:

double quotation mark February is our base case, but the MPC looks willing to pause if the backdrop improves materially. A resolution to the conflict or a further meaningful stabilisation in energy prices would reduce the need for another move, particularly if second-round effects remain limited. So we think the bias is towards another hike in February, but it remains conditional on the energy shock and evidence of persistence.

Daniel Siluk , head of global short duration & liquidity at Janus Henderson Investors , is also cautious about interpreting today’s decision as the beginning of a prolonged hiking cycle.

double quotation mark The energy shock is lifting headline inflation, but there remains relatively limited evidence that it is becoming embedded in broader wages and prices. At the same time, higher energy bills, elevated mortgage rates and tighter financial conditions are increasingly weighing on household purchasing power and should ultimately slow demand. Andrew Bailey was careful to stress that today’s move should not be viewed as the first in a sequence of increases. Our view is that the Bank is effectively buying some insurance against second-round inflation effects and protecting its inflation-fighting credibility. One further increase looks increasingly plausible, but the bigger question for markets is whether the considerably longer tightening cycle currently reflected in the curve will ultimately be delivered.

That was the end of the Bank’s press conference – here’s our news story about the interest rate hike:

Bailey: Burnham right to see opportunity to end Iran and Ukraine wars after midterms

Q: You say the best thing that can happen is, is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East. Given the events of the last 48 hours, would you make that plea directly to US President Donald Trump or the Republican Party for the sake of the UK economy or global economy? (asks Hannah Brenton of Politico).

Andrew Bailey replies that prime minister Andy Burnham put this pont very clearly in the last 24 hours, speaking at the Commonwealth summit [where the PM said the midterm election results are an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war].

Bailey says he supports Burnham on this issue, explaining:

double quotation mark I mean, he also made the same point about Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine. This is absolutely critically important…. I’m very much speaking in the same vein and very much support what he said.

Q: How mindful of you about the NEET crisis, as you mentionead earlier that lower-paid people who are struggling to find work will be hit the hardest by inflation?

Andrew Bailey replies that the Bank is “very conscious” that there is a section of the population on low pay and section of population that isn’t able to find work.

He insists:

double quotation mark We’re very conscious of the impact that inflation, particularly energy price inflation or inflation that originates in energy prices, has, so we are very conscious of that.

Q: Under your central projection, inflation returns target in the third quarter of 2028. It will then have been above the 2% target for for all but one of the previous seven years – what does that say about the BoE’s credibility as an inflation-targeting central bank?

Bailey blames the series of shocks that have hit the UK economy, arguing that few people would have predicted in 2020 that we would today be living in a world where there is a major war in the Middle East and in Europe at the same time .

Bailey denies trying to influence the budget

Q: Governor, you said before the budget that fiscal policy needed to be directed towards stability, and be seen by markets as credible – did the chancellor get the message?

Andrew Bailey bristles at the suggestion he was trying to influence John Healey’s first budget, saying:

double quotation mark I’m very careful what I say on fiscal policy. I said nothing on the budget whatsoever.

Bailey then deploys the BoE’s monetary policy remit in his defence, saying it gives the Bank the objective of supporting the economic policies of the government of the day, including the fiscal framework.

He insists, firmly:

double quotation mark I do support it. So there’s nothing more to it than that, really. It’s not a controversial thing to say at all. Really.

Asked about UK-EU ties, Bailey bangs drum for trade and openness

Q: The government has talked about wanting to open a new conversation about the UK’s future relationship with the European Union – Do you welcome that conversation? Do you expect to contribute to it? And is the Bank’s broad view that a closer relationship with the EU will be positive for growth? (my colleague Heather Stewart asks).

Andrew Bailey reminds the press conference that he has a long record of not taking a view on Brexit, per se.

But he then argues the merits of greater trade and openness, telling reporters:

double quotation mark I am in favour of trade and openness because it actually is a source of growth and economies. It is a source of productivity growth. We learn this from Adam Smith and ever since and so, anything that is done to enhance and support the development of sustainable trade and openness is something I would encourage.

Q: Does the Bank see any risks from the strength of wage growth in the public sector?

[Reminder: earnings growth is running at 6.3% in the public sector and 3.0% in the private sector, according to the latest data].

Deputy governor Clare Lombardelli says the Bank does not see public sector pay as a particular risk, adding:

double quotation mark Obviously, we’ve had the decision around the living wage – our agents tell us it is in line with what people were expecting or potentially a little below it. So we don’t think that will be an additional pressure .

Acrimony had developed between the two parties over the issue

Published 4 November 2026

The leader of Labour on Sheffield City Council has said a deal would be announced in coming days about continuing a power-sharing deal with the Green Party.

It came after a bitter row over Zionism, which saw Labour nationally telling 11 councils, including Sheffield, to break power deals with the Greens.

Until this afternoon's council meeting, it had been expected that Labour would move to run matters in the city on its own, by ditching power-sharing with the Greens.

Speaking to a delayed full council meeting, Labour leader Fran Belbin said talks had been going on, and a joint statement would be made "in coming days" to show they could continue the current administration.

About 50 protestors shouted slogans and made speeches outside the town hall

A protest was held outside the town hall ahead of the meeting, chiefly by pro- Palestine supporters.

Inside, the full council meeting was delayed for an hour as talks between Labour and the Greens continued.

Once underway, Belbin apologised to councillors for the delay and went on to explain that the two parties would "work more constructively together going forward".

She went on to indicate that a joint statement would soon mean that the current arrangement with the Greens would not change.

The power deal between Labour and the Greens in Sheffield came about following May's local elections, in which no party was left in overall control.

Commenting on the announcement by Belbin, councillor Martin Smith, leader of the Liberal Democrat Group, said: "This is an extraordinary U-turn and a shameful abandonment of principle by Labour.

"Just days ago, Labour were telling us that trust with the Greens was completely broken and that they could no longer work together. Now they've decided to carry on as if nothing happened."

Cost of servicing external debt is preventing developing countries from investing for future

Debt owed by developing countries rose to a record $9.4tn (£7tn) last year, with the poorest paying the highest interest rates since the late 1980s, World Bank data shows.

The UK government is preparing to champion a “new drive on debt” as part of its presidency of the G20 next year – a move the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has linked to confronting the legacy of slavery.

In its annual International Debt Report, the World Bank said the rising cost of servicing external debt was preventing some governments from investing for the future.

The increase in developing country debt last year, of 5.5%, was the fastest in four years, the report finds – driven by a rapid rise in private sector lending.

The World Bank’s chief statistician, Haishan Fu, said: “Access to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not. Low- and middle-income countries are borrowing more, paying more, and, in many cases, leaving less for long-term development.”

On average, the report found the poorest countries – those eligible for concessional lending from the World Bank – faced an average interest rate of 8.2% on new borrowing: the highest since the late 1980s. It also said preliminary data for 2026 suggested lending continued at a rapid pace – but at continued high interest rates as global financing costs rose.

The Bank highlighted recent borrowing by Laos, at an interest rate of 11.5%, the Republic of Congo, at 13.88%, and Kenya, at 9.2%.

Analysing the connection between a high debt burden and the ability to spend on domestic priorities, the World Bank found global shocks had more impact on the availability of food in heavily indebted countries.

“Food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress,” the report said.

after newsletter promotion

Burnham has appointed the former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown to examine the feasibility of changes to the global debt regime in the run-up to the UK’s G20 presidency next year.

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, set out plans last month for a “new deal” for heavily indebted countries in a speech at the IMF annual meetings in Bangkok. The deal is likely to include proposals to mobilise the balance sheets of the World Bank and other multilateral development banks to buy back outstanding debt in an effort to extend repayment periods and bring down interest rates.

However, the situation is more complex than in the run-up to the Gleneagles summit in 2005 – when G8 countries signed up to write off billions of pounds worth of debt – because today’s creditors tend to be private-sector bondholders, not governments.

There have been growing demands in recent years for changes to the framework for international debt, including from African Union heads of state , and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.

As Wall Street sustained widespread losses, the Nasdaq composite tumbled into “correction territory” – more than 10% below its recent record high – with more than $2tn shaved off its value by the end of trading Thursday. The tech-heavy index had its biggest one-day fall since Donald Trump announced his “liberation day” tariffs on US trading partners in April 2025.

Worries over massive AI spending gripped the New York stock market and rippled out to other bourses worldwide as investors anticipated tougher scrutiny of datacentre expansion plans.

Chip stocks led the slump, with memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%.

Wall Street’s “fear index”, the VIX, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.

Analysts pointed to expectations that Democratic governors will clamp down on the rollout of new datacentres after the party won a series of gubernatorial races this week. US voters also rejected datacentres in a series of local ballots across the country.

Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK, said a “complete capitulation-level event” was playing out in tech stocks on Thursday.

“The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh datacentre buildout … this looks totally overdone but the nature of ‘sell everything’ in this market means we need to look for some stability first,” Wilson said.

The Dow Jones industrial average (DJIA) of 30 large US companies was down more than 1,800 points by the end of the day, a fall of 3.4%, to 51,868 points. The S&P 500 was down 4.3%.

Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom, was the top faller on the DJIA – down 9.2%, followed by Goldman Sachs, which fell 3.7%.

An early stock market rally in Europe had fizzled out by late trading, with Britain’s FTSE 100 closing down 46 points or 0.4% at 10782.66.

The sell-off is a sharp reverse of Wednesday’s rally, when Wall Street stocks had their biggest daily gain in months as investors anticipated that the Democratic party’s success in the US midterm elections could restrain the White House.

That rally prompted Donald Trump to once again boast about the record-breaking highs the stock markets had reached during his second term. The president wrote on Truth Social: “Stock Market just hit another Record High – 91 Days in just a short period of time — Less than two years. Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Tech analyst Dan Ives has warned that the results of the midterms are a clear sign that the pace of datacentre buildout will start to slow down.

“There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next two years,” Ives said.

“The market’s moving from the promise ⁠of AI to the price of AI,” said Ted Parkhill, founder and CEO of Incline ​Investment Management.

“There’s no question that AI is ​going to be transformative for the world in ​the long run. But that doesn’t mean every AI-related stock is currently priced appropriately. There’s going to be ​a lot of turmoil.”

stories.summary: Bad job interviews can be horrible to experience in the moment, but there is a lot they can teach us about the world of work
